Release audit fix round 4, 18 Nov 2026: key no longer echoes the stem's 'model's'; stem asks which stratum concentrates the model's wrong levels, so caseload peaks (same error share, fewer checks) no longer read as a second answer. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing automatic approvals
questions.question: A Beninese cotton board's model auto-approves farmers' input-subsidy claims with risk scores below 0.2 and sends the rest to officers. Which population BEST supports the IS auditor's test of whether auto-approval works?

options.A: Auto-approved claims, each checked against farm and delivery records
options.B: Claims officers reviewed, compared with their final decisions
options.C: Claims later found fraudulent, traced back to their model scores
options.D: Past claims with known outcomes, rescored by the current model

questions.key_concept: To test automated approval, sample the auto-approved items against independent records; known failures exclude everything nobody detected.
questions.pre_read: Find the decisions no person reviews, and ask where their errors would show.
questions.correct_explanation: Auto-approval is the part no person checks, so its effectiveness shows only in auto-approved claims tested against independent records. Claims later found fraudulent are useful, but they are only the cases someone happened to detect; fraud inside auto-approved claims that nobody caught never reaches that list. Officer-reviewed claims test the referral path, not auto-approval.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because officer decisions are a ready check. But referred claims show how risky cases are handled, not what auto-approval let through.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because they are confirmed errors. But detected fraud is only the fraud someone caught; undetected cases in auto-approved claims stay outside it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outcomes are known. But past claims rescored today test the current model on old data, not what auto-approval did this year.

tips: Eliminate: B tests the path officers already review, and D rescores old claims rather than testing this year's approvals.
Final two: A beats C because detected fraud includes only what someone caught; testing auto-approved claims against records can find what nobody caught.
Exam cue: to test an automated decision, sample what it decided without a person. Known failures are leads, never the full population.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF Guideline 2208 (Information Technology Audit Sampling); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.2 Sampling AI Decisions (design an AI sample around where errors hide; define the population as the production decisions in scope). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reperforming from a feature store
questions.question: To reperform a Bruneian buy-now-pay-later provider's spending-limit renewals, the IS auditor plans to pull sampled customers' features from the feature store and score them with the archived version that decided. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The store may hold today's values, not those used when deciding
options.B: The archived version may not read the store's current feature format
options.C: The sample may hold too few large limit cuts to compare groups
options.D: The archived version differs from the model now in production

questions.key_concept: Reperformance needs the deciding model version and the inputs as they were at decision time; current feature values change the case.
questions.pre_read: List each part of the planned rerun and compare it with the original decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Reperforming a decision needs the model version that made it and the inputs as they were then. A feature store often keeps each customer's latest values, such as missed repayments and monthly spending, so today's features would have the archived version score a different case. The rerun could then disagree, or agree, for the wrong reason, with nothing to warn the auditor. A format mismatch fails visibly and can be fixed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because feature formats change over time. But a format mismatch fails visibly and can be fixed; stale inputs fail silently and corrupt every comparison.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because group comparisons need enough cases. But the objective is reperforming decisions, not fairness; sample design does not fix wrong inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because versions differ. But using the deciding version is the right choice; the current model would be the wrong one.

tips: Eliminate: D names the correct choice of model as a problem, and C raises a fairness question this test does not ask.
Final two: A beats B because current feature values silently change the case being scored; a format mismatch fails visibly.
Exam cue: reperforming an AI decision needs the deciding version and the inputs as they were then. Ask whether each input is a point-in-time record.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.3 Reperformance and Full-Population Testing (a logged decision can be reproduced only if the same model version and the same inputs are still available). Setting changed in batch 4 completeness round 1: a motor insurer's renewal-premium model repeated crisc_d2_025's insurer ML pricing setting; now a buy-now-pay-later provider's spending-limit renewals, angle and key unchanged. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Challenger model results
questions.question: An IS auditor's independently built challenger model disagrees with a Kazakh steel mill's scrap-grading model on 7% of 30,000 scrap loads. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Report the 7% disagreement as the grading model's error rate
options.B: Treat the loads where both models agree as correctly graded
options.C: Recommend retraining the grading model on the challenger's grades
options.D: Check a sample of disagreeing loads against independent expert grades

questions.key_concept: A challenger model's disagreements are leads; the auditor verifies a sample against an independent source before measuring errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask which source, other than either model, shows the right grade.
questions.correct_explanation: A challenger model is another model, not the truth. Disagreements show where one of the two is likely wrong, so they are leads: checking a sample against independent expert grades shows which model erred and how often. Reporting 7% as the grading model's error rate assumes the challenger is right every time, when it may be the one making the mistakes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the challenger was built independently. But independence is not accuracy; until disagreements are checked, the 7% could be the challenger's errors.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agreement feels like confirmation. But two models trained on similar data can share the same errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to fix the gap. But retraining design belongs to the model owner, and the challenger's grades are unverified.

tips: Eliminate: B treats agreement between two models as proof, and C has the auditor steering the owner's model fix.
Final two: D beats A because a challenger's disagreement is a lead; only independent expert grades show which model graded each load wrongly.
Exam cue: an audit challenger model points testing at likely errors. Its outputs are leads to verify, not a measure of the production model's accuracy.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.3 Reperformance and Full-Population Testing (an independent challenger model can show where outputs diverge and point testing at likely errors). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Evidence of a threshold change
questions.question: A Sierra Leonean energy agency's solar-rebate approvals halved in June; its screening model's version log shows no release since January. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether, and by whom, the cutoff was altered?

options.A: The model card's stated cutoff score for rebate approvals
options.B: June's decision log showing each applicant's score and outcome
options.C: The scoring platform's settings history for the cutoff value
options.D: The model version log naming who approved each release

questions.key_concept: AI thresholds are configuration that can change without a new model version; settings history, not the version log, shows such changes.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the trained model holds from what is set around it.
questions.correct_explanation: A cutoff is usually a platform setting rather than part of the trained model, so it can be altered without a new model version. The platform's settings history for that value shows whether, when and by whom the cutoff moved. June's decision log lets the auditor infer an effective cutoff from scores and outcomes, but cannot prove the setting was altered, or show who altered it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the cutoff. But a model card is the builders' description and may never have been updated after a settings change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scores and outcomes reveal the effective cutoff. But inference shows a pattern, not the change itself, when it happened or who made it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it records approvers and shows no release since January. But a cutoff set on the platform can move without a new version, so this log cannot show it.

tips: Eliminate: A is the builders' description, which may predate any change, and D records model releases, while a platform cutoff can move without one.
Final two: C beats B because the settings history records the change itself; decision logs only let the auditor infer one.
Exam cue: a model's threshold can change without a new version. Ask for the configuration history, not just the model version log.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.1 Sources of AI Evidence (decision, override and prompt logs, with model version and configuration history, show what happened in production; match the evidence to the question). Setting changed in batch 4 completeness round 1: a university's admissions scoring model repeated crisc_d1_004's admissions setting; the aid agency's cash-transfer eligibility model that replaced it repeated aaia_d2_034's aid-agency entitlement setting; a fisheries ministry was proposed but aaia_d1_055 already uses one, so now an energy agency's solar-rebate screening model, angle and key unchanged. Stem says 'altered' and option C says 'settings history' so the key no longer echoes the stem's wording. Principle moved from ai-changes-are-changes (domains omit D3) to reproducible-ai-evidence: the settings history is the exact-settings record, the decision log only an inference. Option D changed in the batch 4 re-audit from the January validation report to the model version log naming approvers, so the key is no longer the only option that names who acted and the stem's version-log fact becomes a live trap. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Use beyond validated limits
questions.question: A Quebec dental chain's cavity-detection model card says it was validated on adult X-rays only. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether the model is used beyond that limit?

options.A: The validation report describing the X-rays in its test data
options.B: Production scan logs recording each patient's age band
options.C: Booking rules that send children to dentists not using the model
options.D: The clinical lead's statement on which patients the model reads

questions.key_concept: Whether an AI model is used beyond its validated limits shows in production records, compared with the model card's stated limits.
questions.pre_read: Ask which record shows whose X-rays the model actually read.
questions.correct_explanation: The question is how the model is actually used, so the evidence is production records of whose X-rays it read. Scan logs with each patient's age band show whether children's X-rays went through the model despite the adult-only validation. Booking rules show a control's design, but bookings change and walk-ins happen, so rules cannot show which X-rays the model really read.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it defines the validated population. But it shows which X-rays were tested before release, not which the model reads now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks like a preventive control. But a rule shows design; only production records show whose X-rays actually reached the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the clinical lead knows the practice. But a statement of intended use is inquiry, the weakest evidence of actual use.

tips: Eliminate: A shows what was tested before release, and D is a person's account rather than a record of use.
Final two: B beats C because scan logs show whose X-rays the model read; booking rules show only how use was meant to be limited.
Exam cue: to check use against a model card's limits, compare the card with production records. Rules and intentions show design, not use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.3 (Targeted application scope specified); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.1 Sources of AI Evidence (model cards state intended use and limits; compare the model card's stated limits with observed production use). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Evidence of retraining approval
questions.question: A Djiboutian bank's trade-finance fraud model can be retrained and promoted to production automatically by its pipeline. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor that every retrained version was approved before use?

options.A: Inquiry of the model owner about the approval steps
options.B: A walkthrough of the next planned retraining and its approval
options.C: The pipeline's gate that blocks promotion unless validation tests pass
options.D: The model registry's version history, matched to approvals

questions.key_concept: Pipelines can promote retrained models with no human sign-off; match the registry's version history to approvals, since passing the builders' test gate is not approval.
questions.pre_read: Separate a pipeline checking metrics from a person approving a model.
questions.correct_explanation: When a pipeline can promote models by itself, the question is whether someone with authority approved each version before it went live. The model registry is where the pipeline records each version it promotes, so matching its history to approval records tests the whole period. A validation gate shows the pipeline checks builders' metrics; passing those tests is not the owner's approval, and the gate's design says nothing about versions already promoted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner knows the process. But inquiry is the weakest evidence and cannot show what the pipeline did on its own.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it observes the process. But one walkthrough shows a single future event, not whether every past version was approved.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an automated preventive control looks strong. But passing builders' validation tests is not an owner's approval, and the gate's design shows nothing about past versions.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on inquiry alone, and B observes one future retrain rather than the period under audit.
Final two: D beats C because approval is a person accepting each version; a gate that checks metrics is the builders' test, and its design shows nothing about past promotions.
Exam cue: when AI pipelines retrain and deploy on their own, test approval across the model registry's history. A passed test gate is not an approval.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.2 Sufficiency, Reliability and Preservation of AI Evidence (evidence must cover the whole period under audit; a builders' test gate is not approval of a retrained version). Principle moved in batch 4 completeness round 1 from ai-changes-are-changes (domains omit D3) to independence-of-ai-assurance: the runner-up is the builders' own validation gate offered as approval. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Records of an agent's actions
questions.question: To test which customer accounts an Eswatini electricity company's AI agent changed, the IS auditor is offered the agent's own end-of-day summaries of its actions. Which evidence is MOST reliable?

options.A: The billing system's audit trail of changes by the agent's account
options.B: The agent's summaries, checked by asking it to relist its changes
options.C: The supervisor's daily sign-off on each of the agent's summaries
options.D: The permissions configured for the agent's customer account changes

questions.key_concept: An AI agent's summaries of its own actions are self-reports; the target system's audit trail is the reliable record.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced each record: the agent, a person reading the agent, or the system acted on.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's summary is its own account of what it did, and generated text can omit or misstate actions. The billing system's audit trail records every change made under the agent's account, independent of what the agent says. A supervisor's sign-off adds a review, but the supervisor signs the same self-report and has no independent record to compare it with.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems to double-check. But asking the agent again tests its consistency, not its accuracy; it can repeat the same omissions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because management review is a control. But the supervisor reviews the agent's self-report, so the sign-off inherits its gaps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because permissions bound the agent. But they show what it could change, not what it actually changed.

tips: Eliminate: B asks the agent to check itself, and D shows what the agent could change rather than what it did.
Final two: A beats C because the system's audit trail records changes independently; a supervisor signing the agent's summary still relies on the agent's own account.
Exam cue: an AI agent's report of its own actions is a lead. The record of what it did lives in the systems it acted on.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.2 Sufficiency, Reliability and Preservation of AI Evidence (rank evidence: what the auditor reperforms or a system produces, then documents, then statements; prefer records over time). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Checking an AI summary
questions.question: An IS auditor confirmed that every statement in an approved AI tool's summary of a Timor-Leste ministry's 90-page IT risk register appears in the register. What is the GREATEST remaining concern?

options.A: A rerun of the same prompt might give a different summary
options.B: The summary might leave out risks the register rates high
options.C: The vendor might keep the register to train its models
options.D: The tool's confidence score for the summary was not recorded

questions.key_concept: Tracing an AI summary's statements to the source catches invented content but not omissions; check important source items against the summary too.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the check performed can and cannot detect.
questions.correct_explanation: Tracing each statement to the register tests what the summary says, so invented content is ruled out. It cannot test what the summary left out, and summarizing tools often drop items, including high-rated risks the audit plan depends on. Comparing the register's high-rated risks with the summary closes that gap. A rerun that differs is a reproducibility issue; it does not show this summary is incomplete.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reruns can vary. But variation is handled by recording run conditions; it says nothing about whether this summary omitted risks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit data must stay confidential. But the tool is approved, so its data terms were already assessed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confidence feels like quality. But a tool's self-rating is not evidence, and recording it would not reveal omissions.

tips: Eliminate: C reopens data terms the tool's approval already covered, and D relies on the tool's rating of itself.
Final two: B beats A because tracing statements catches inventions, not omissions; a summary can be accurate in every line and still drop key risks.
Exam cue: verify AI output both ways: is each statement in the source, and is each important source item in the output?
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.3 Evidence Produced by AI Tools (treat AI output as a lead until corroborated against source records; AI tools can misread, omit or invent content). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An auditee's AI-produced review
questions.question: A Bavarian auto-parts maker's IT team says its generative AI assistant, whose answers can vary between runs, reviewed all 1,200 access changes against approvals and found no exceptions. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the assistant's review of the 1,200 access changes against approvals
options.B: Ask the assistant's vendor for its published accuracy rate
options.C: Test a sample of the access changes against the approval records
options.D: Test the assistant's prompts, settings and change controls, then rely on it

questions.key_concept: An auditee's AI-produced control review is management's assertion; the auditor obtains direct evidence by testing the underlying records.
questions.pre_read: Ask who ran the tool and whose conclusion its result is.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant's result is the IT team's own review, produced with a tool the auditee runs and prompts, so it is management's assertion, not the auditor's own evidence. Testing a sample of changes against approval records gives direct evidence. Testing the prompts, settings and change controls, as one would a report's logic and general controls, feels thorough, but an assistant whose answers vary between runs can misjudge any change however sound and controlled its prompts.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because full coverage sounds strong. But the review was run by the auditee with its own tool; coverage claimed is not coverage tested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy matters. But a vendor's figure comes from other data and says nothing about this review.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing logic and change controls is how auditors rely on system output. But a generative assistant can misjudge any change however sound its prompts; only records show it.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the auditee's own claim of full coverage, and B relies on a vendor figure from other data.

Final two: C beats D because testing prompts and change controls tests the assistant's design, but a generative tool can misjudge any change; testing changes against approval records gives direct evidence.
Exam cue: an auditee's AI-produced review is a management assertion. Test the underlying records; sound prompts do not make each generated judgment right.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.3 Evidence Produced by AI Tools (AI output is a lead until corroborated against source records; evidence the auditor cannot trace to source records cannot support a conclusion). Release audit, 18 Nov 2026: runner-up D now inspects the assistant's prompts and settings, which only the generative-AI fact defeats. Release audit fix round 2, 18 Nov 2026: runner-up D now also tests change controls, the CISA route to relying on system output, which only the generative-AI fact defeats; 'directly' removed from the key. Release audit final round, 18 Nov 2026: stem now says the assistant is generative, the fact the explanation relies on. Release audit fix round 4, 18 Nov 2026: stem says the assistant's answers can vary between runs, the fact that defeats relying on its prompts and change controls. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Model-replaced values in audit data
questions.question: Recomputing a Surinamese ministry's childcare-subsidy approval rates by stated income band, an IS auditor learns a data-warehouse cleaning model judged 18% of incomes implausible and replaced them with estimates. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Exclude the 18% with estimated incomes from the recomputation
options.B: Use the extract, since the data team validated its cleaning model
options.C: Obtain the incomes applicants stated from the application system
options.D: Ask the data team to document why stated incomes were replaced

questions.key_concept: Values a model imputed or replaced are estimates, not source records; the auditor obtains source values rather than testing or dropping estimates.
questions.pre_read: Ask which values in the extract came from people and which came from a model.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's estimates are not source data: replaced incomes show what a cleaning model guessed, not what applicants stated, so they can move people between income bands. The auditor goes back to the application system for the recorded incomes. Excluding the 18% looks cautious, but values judged implausible may cluster among some applicants, such as the self-employed, so dropping them can distort the very rates being compared.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids estimated values. But the replaced records may not be random, so dropping them can skew approval rates by band.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the cleaning model was validated. But validation shows it estimates well on average, not that estimates equal each applicant's stated income.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because understanding the replacements helps. But documentation explains why values changed without restoring the incomes applicants stated.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a validated estimate as the recorded value, and D documents why values changed instead of restoring the source values.
Final two: C beats A because the source holds the stated incomes; dropping the replaced 18% can skew the income bands being compared.
Exam cue: when a model has filled in or replaced values in audit data, go back to the source. Model estimates are not records.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.1 Completeness and Accuracy of Audit Data (the data the auditor tests holds every relevant record, unchanged from the source; populations can be shaped upstream by filters or a model). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI-written extract query
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI assistant wrote the query extracting a Belizean tourism board's tour-guide licensing decisions; the assistant then queried the source system for a total, which matched. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Compare the extract to a total from the system's own reports
options.B: Rely on the match, since the total came from the source system
options.C: Accept the extract, since the assistant is approved for audit use
options.D: Ask the assistant to explain what each of its queries does

questions.key_concept: A reconciliation is independent only if the source total comes from outside the AI tool that wrote the extract query.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced each of the two numbers being compared.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant wrote both queries, so the match checks its work against itself: an AI-written query can drop records through a wrong join, filter or date range, and the same misreading of the schema can shape the total too. A total the assistant did not produce, such as the system's own report, gives an independent check. A source-system figure is independent only when the query behind it is.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the total came from the source system. But the assistant wrote that query too, so one wrong filter or date range can shape both numbers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tool passed the audit function's approval. But approval permits using the tool; it does not show this query returned every record.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to check the logic. But the assistant explaining its own queries can repeat its own mistake.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the tool's approval as proof of this one output, and D asks the tool to check its own work.
Final two: A beats B because a total the same assistant queried is not independent; one misread schema can drop the same records from both counts.
Exam cue: reconcile AI-written extracts to a figure the AI tool did not shape. A total the same assistant queried checks its work against itself.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.1 Completeness and Accuracy of Audit Data (an extract is a copy; queries, joins and date ranges can drop records without any error message; reconcile counts and totals to the source). Re-angled at the batch 4 cross-domain gate: the earlier key (reconcile to the source) was answerable from CISA alone; the deciding fact is now that a source total the same assistant queried is not independent. Option A reworded in batch 4 round 2 so the key is not the only negated option. Stem reworded in batch 4 round 3 to make explicit that the assistant, not the auditor, queried the total. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Scoring an audit tool
questions.question: A Faroese salmon exporter's audit team tuned its AI duplicate-invoice tool on 200 known duplicates, then reported it found 196 of them. What is the GREATEST concern with relying on this result?

options.A: Two hundred known duplicates are too few to tune the tool
options.B: The four missed duplicates were not examined for a common pattern
options.C: The tool vendor's own published accuracy figure was not checked
options.D: The tool was scored on the same cases used to tune it

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool scored on the cases used to tune it overstates performance; validation needs known cases held back from tuning.
questions.pre_read: Read how the result was produced before trusting the number.
questions.correct_explanation: Scoring a tool on the cases used to tune it is like grading an exam the student has already seen: the 98% shows how well it fits those 200, not how many new duplicates it will catch. Validation needs known cases held back from tuning. Studying the four misses could refine the tool, but it still trusts a catch rate that overstates performance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small tuning sets can limit a tool. But the bigger flaw is scoring it on those same cases, which inflates the result whatever the set's size.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because exceptions deserve follow-up. But the four misses come from the tuning cases; the 98% itself overstates what the tool will catch on new invoices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors publish figures. But a vendor figure from other data would not validate the tool here either.

tips: Eliminate: C looks to a vendor figure that cannot validate the tool on this data, and A blames the set's size rather than how it was scored.
Final two: D beats B because studying four misses still trusts a catch rate measured on tuning cases; only known cases held back from tuning show what the tool will miss.
Exam cue: validate an audit AI tool on known cases it never saw while being tuned, just as models are tested on held-out data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.2 AI-Assisted Audit Analytics and Tool Validation (validate the tool before relying on it by running it on data whose correct answers are known; measure both errors). Release audit fix round 2, 18 Nov 2026: runner-up B now examines the four misses instead of false alarms, removing a second defensible gap and the false-alarm runner-up shared with aaia_d3_106. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Setting an audit tool's threshold
questions.question: Validating its anomaly tool on known cases, a Guyanese gold exporter's audit team finds a higher threshold cuts false alarms by 80% but raises missed fraud from 5% to 30%. Which threshold choice is BEST?

options.A: Adopt the higher threshold, since follow-up effort falls by 80%
options.B: Set the threshold from the engagement's tolerable miss rate
options.C: Keep the vendor's default threshold to avoid any tuning bias
options.D: Adopt the higher threshold and disclose the 30% miss rate

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's threshold trades false alarms against misses; the team sets it from the miss rate the engagement objective can tolerate.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each error costs this engagement before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A threshold trades false alarms against misses, so the choice follows what the engagement must not miss. For fraud testing at a gold exporter, a tool missing 30% of known fraud may not support the planned conclusion, so the team sets the threshold from the miss rate the objective can tolerate and plans other tests for the rest. Disclosing a 30% miss rate is honest, but it does not make an unsupportable conclusion supportable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because false alarms consume effort. But effort saved is not the objective; missing almost a third of known fraud undermines reliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids the team's own choices. But the vendor's default was not set for this data or this engagement's risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is transparent. But disclosure explains a weakness; it does not give enough evidence for a fraud conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: A sets the threshold by effort rather than by the objective, and C defers to a default chosen for other data.
Final two: B beats D because the threshold must fit what the engagement can afford to miss; disclosing a high miss rate does not make reliance supportable.
Exam cue: an audit AI tool's threshold is an audit judgment. Measure both error types, then set it by the misses the objective can tolerate.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.1 (Methods and metrics selected starting with the most significant risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.2 AI-Assisted Audit Analytics and Tool Validation (measure both errors: false positives waste effort, while false negatives let real exceptions pass unseen). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Tuning on work papers
questions.question: A North Macedonian state railway's audit function plans to fine-tune its approved language model on five years of work papers, including staff disciplinary records, to draft findings in house style. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The tuned model may repeat personal details in other auditors' drafts
options.B: The tuned model will need validation before its drafts are relied on
options.C: Five years of work papers may carry an outdated house style
options.D: Fine-tuning may cost more than writing a house style guide

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning on work papers can make a model memorize and later reproduce confidential personal data, a confidentiality risk beyond output quality.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the training data goes once a model has been tuned on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuned models can memorize parts of their training text and reproduce it when prompted, so disciplinary records in the work papers could surface in drafts for other engagements and users without a need to know. That is a confidentiality harm to named staff that no later review can undo. Validating the tuned model before reliance is needed too, but review catches a quality gap; it cannot recall a disclosure.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because any audit AI tool is validated before reliance. But validation checks draft quality; it does not stop memorized personal data from leaking.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because style changes. But an outdated style is a quality nuisance, fixable in review, not a harm to people.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cost matters. But cost is a business choice; exposing disciplinary records harms staff and the audit function's credibility.

tips: Eliminate: C is a style problem that review fixes, and D is a cost choice rather than a risk to people.
Final two: A beats B because memorized personal data can leak into later drafts; validation tests draft quality but cannot recall a disclosure.
Exam cue: training or tuning on audit data puts that data inside the model. Ask what personal or confidential content could resurface, and to whom.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3.2 (Information Extraction); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.3 Reproducibility and Confidentiality in AI-Assisted Audits (keep audit data inside approved tools; data used to train a model can be exposed later). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. An AI service's web-search feature
questions.question: A Greenlandic municipality's audit team finds its approved AI service's web-search feature sends prompt text to a search provider outside the contract. What should the chief audit executive do FIRST?

options.A: Allow its use, since the main service is approved under contract
options.B: Strip names from any prompt that might trigger a web search
options.C: Ask the vendor to confirm the search provider deletes queries
options.D: Disable web search for audit work until its data path is assessed

questions.key_concept: An AI service's approval covers data paths its contract covers; features that send audit data to outside providers need assessment first.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the audit data goes when the feature runs.
questions.correct_explanation: The approval covered the AI service under its contract terms; the search feature sends audit data to a provider those terms do not cover, so the approval does not extend to it. Disabling the feature for audit work keeps data inside the approved boundary while the path is assessed. Stripping names leaves context that can still identify people and does nothing for confidential findings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the service is approved. But approval rested on contract terms that do not reach the outside search provider.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it reduces personal data. But context can still identify people, and confidential audit facts leave anyway.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seeks assurance. But a vendor's word about a provider outside the contract is not an enforceable term.

tips: Eliminate: A extends an approval past the contract it rested on, and C relies on a vendor's word with no contract behind it.
Final two: D beats B because the feature sends audit data outside the approved boundary; stripping names still lets confidential findings and context leave.
Exam cue: an approved AI service is approved under its terms. A feature that sends data elsewhere is outside the approval until assessed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.3 Reproducibility and Confidentiality in AI-Assisted Audits (contract terms and data classification decide which audit data an AI service may receive; removing names does not make data safe). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Effect of a precision drop
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the precision of a Papua New Guinean electoral commission's model, which flags voter-roll entries as duplicates for removal, fell from 0.88 to 0.61. Which statement BEST describes the finding's effect?

options.A: The model now misses more of the duplicate entries it should flag
options.B: Nearly four in ten flagged entries may be genuine voters struck off
options.C: Voter-roll data may have drifted from the model's training data
options.D: No alert limit was set for a fall in the model's precision

questions.key_concept: A finding's effect translates the AI metric into consequences: falling precision means more false flags acted on, not more missed cases.
questions.pre_read: Define the metric in plain words before choosing what it means for people.
questions.correct_explanation: Precision is the share of flagged entries that really are duplicates, so a fall to 0.61 means about 39% of flags now point at genuine, separate voters who could be wrongly removed from the roll. That is the effect in human terms. Saying the model misses more duplicates describes recall, which a precision figure does not measure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missed duplicates sound like the risk. But that is recall; a precision figure shows wrong flags, not how many duplicates went unflagged.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because drift often lowers precision. But drift is a mechanism, not the effect, and nothing in the finding establishes it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it names a control gap. But a missing alert limit is the cause; the effect is what the decline does to voters.

tips: Eliminate: C explains how the decline might happen, and D names the control gap, which is the cause.
Final two: B beats A because precision measures how many flags are right; how many duplicates were missed is recall, which this figure cannot show.
Exam cue: translate an AI metric before writing its effect. Precision counts actions taken on false flags; recall counts real cases missed.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.1 Writing AI Audit Findings (effect is the consequence for people and the business; a metric decline is the condition, not the effect). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Cause of an agent's overweight bookings
questions.question: A Vanuatu freight airline's AI booking agent accepted 40 shipments above the 70 kg parcel limit in its instructions; the cargo system enforces no weight cap. Which cause should the IS auditor report as PRIMARY?

options.A: The agent's model misread or ignored the weight limit in its instructions
options.B: Staff did not check the cargo system's bookings against the cap
options.C: The limit relied on instructions, with no cap in the cargo system
options.D: A vendor model update changed how the agent follows its instructions

questions.key_concept: When an AI agent breaks a limit held only in its prompt, the reportable cause is the missing system-enforced control, not the model's disobedience.
questions.pre_read: Find where the limit was enforced, if anywhere.
questions.correct_explanation: An instruction in an agent's prompt is guidance the model may misread, ignore or be manipulated into breaking, so it is not a control. The control gap is that nothing outside the model enforced the 70 kg cap in the cargo system. That the model disobeyed is the mechanism; even a model that usually obeys would leave bookings unprotected against misreading or manipulation.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model broke its instruction. But that is how the failure happened; the cause is relying on an instruction no system enforced.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review would catch overweight bookings. But review detects after acceptance; the gap that let the shipments through is the missing enforced cap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor updates can change behavior. But nothing in the facts points to an update; the stated gap is the unenforced limit.

tips: Eliminate: D blames an update the facts never mention, and B names a later check rather than the gap that let the shipments through.
Final two: C beats A because a prompt instruction is not a control; the model disobeying is the mechanism, the unenforced cap is the cause.
Exam cue: when an AI agent exceeds a limit, look for where the limit lived. A limit held only in the prompt is the control gap to report.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.1 Writing AI Audit Findings (cause is named as the control gap; the mechanism of failure is not the cause). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. An overdue AI action
questions.question: An Uzbek pension fund's 99%-accurate model suspends pensions of members flagged as deceased; its agreed human-review step is nine months overdue, and the model now covers every region. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Agree a revised date for the overdue step, given the 99% accuracy
options.B: Direct the model owner to pause suspensions until review starts
options.C: Design the human-review step for the model owner to put in place
options.D: Report the late action and its wider exposure to the audit committee

questions.key_concept: Overdue actions on high-impact AI findings go to the audit committee with their exposure; high accuracy does not offset harm at scale.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the overdue step protects, how far the model now reaches and what 99% leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: A high-impact AI control is nine months late while the model's reach has grown to every region. A 99% accuracy figure does not offset that: at national scale, a small error rate still suspends many living members' pensions with no person checking. Overdue actions of this impact go to the audit committee with the wider exposure; the auditor reports, senior management decides the response and the committee oversees it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because 99% accuracy sounds safe. But at national scale a small error rate still wrongly suspends many living members; a quietly reset date hides that from the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wrong suspensions harm members. But pausing the model is management's decision; the auditor reports the exposure so management and the committee can act.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would speed the fix. But designing the control makes the auditor part of management, impairing objectivity.

tips: Eliminate: B has the auditor directing management to stop the model, and C has the auditor designing management's control.
Final two: D beats A because a small error rate across every region still harms many members while the action slips; leaders must see that, not a quietly reset date.
Exam cue: when an AI fix is overdue and the model's reach grows, report both to the audit committee. High accuracy does not offset harm at scale.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1402 (Follow-up Activities); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.2 (Treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and resources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.2 Rating, Reporting and Follow-Up of AI Findings (record management's response with owners and dates; report overdue actions to the audit committee; rate by likelihood and impact on people). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. A fix that removes a field
questions.question: An Angolan mobile-money lender's loan model declined rural applicants far more often; management removed the home-province field and asks to close the finding. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Applicants may be scored less accurately without the field
options.B: Other inputs may still reveal where applicants live
options.C: The removal may have gone live without change approval
options.D: Management, not the IS auditor, chose how to fix the model

questions.key_concept: Removing a sensitive field does not remove bias carried by proxies; a fairness finding closes on group outcomes, not on the feature list.
questions.pre_read: Read the finding as an outcome, then ask whether the action taken is sure to change that outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Removing a field does not remove what it carried: phone type, top-up locations or language can still stand in for where applicants live, so rural applicants may still be declined far more often. The finding closes only when rural and urban decline rates since the change show the gap has gone. Less accurate scoring is a trade-off for the owner to weigh, not evidence the unfair outcome ended.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing an input can cost accuracy. But that is the owner's trade-off; the finding concerns rural declines, which proxies may keep high.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because model changes need approval. But nothing suggests the change bypassed control; the open question is whether the bias is gone.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it sounds like a gap. But choosing the fix is management's role; the IS auditor verifies whether it worked.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes a change-control gap nothing points to, and D objects to management choosing its own fix, which is its role.
Final two: B beats A because other inputs can carry what the removed field did, so the rural gap may persist; lower accuracy is the owner's trade-off.
Exam cue: removing a sensitive field is not a fairness fix by itself. Expect proxies, and close bias findings on group outcomes since the change.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1402 (Follow-up Activities); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.2 Rating, Reporting and Follow-Up of AI Findings (close findings only on production evidence that the fix resolved what was reported; removing an input does not prove a model fair). Re-angled at the batch 4 cross-domain gate: the earlier version (which evidence closes it: group outcomes since the change) repeated aaia_d3_020 and the 3E.2 notes example. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Tool rating versus observation
questions.question: Three days' observation shows Isle of Man bank staff bulk-clearing a payment model's flags unread; the audit's AI tool, reading only flag statuses, rates the review effective. Which conclusion is BEST for the IS auditor?

options.A: The control is ineffective, with a note on why the tool disagrees
options.B: Accept the tool's rating, since it analyzed the whole year's population
options.C: Report both ratings and let management decide which one applies
options.D: Rerun the tool with revised prompts until its rating matches

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's rating is an input; when direct evidence contradicts it, the auditor concludes on the evidence and documents why.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool could see in its data and what only observation could see.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool read only flag statuses, and a flag cleared unread has the same status as one reviewed with care. Observation shows the review does not operate as intended, and the auditor owns the conclusion. Noting why the tool's rating differs keeps the work papers defensible. Full-population coverage cannot outweigh evidence the data never captured.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because full-population analytics sound stronger than three days of observation. But the tool saw only statuses; a flag cleared unread looks the same as one reviewed with care.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems balanced. But the conclusion is the auditor's to reach; management does not choose the audit's ratings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a better prompt may help. But tuning a tool until it agrees is not evidence; observation already shows the failure.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the audit's conclusion to management, and D adjusts the tool until it gives the wanted answer.
Final two: A beats B because the tool judged only flag statuses; an unread clearance has the same status as a careful one, so the auditor's evidence decides.
Exam cue: an audit AI tool's rating is input, never the conclusion. When direct evidence contradicts it, conclude on the evidence and record why they differ.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.3 Disclosing AI Use and Owning Conclusions (never present an AI tool's output as a conclusion without the auditor's own judgment; the auditor stays accountable for every finding). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. AI-drafted recommendation
questions.question: Reviewing AI-drafted report text on a Gabonese timber firm's injury-risk model, an IS audit manager sees a recommendation telling the model owner to retrain with a named oversampling method. What is the manager's BEST response?

options.A: Keep the method, since it is a sound fix for the model
options.B: Keep the method, and disclose that an AI tool drafted it
options.C: Reword it as an outcome, leaving the method to the owner
options.D: Ask the owner to trial the method before the report is issued

questions.key_concept: Audit recommendations on AI state the result or control needed; the model owner chooses the technical fix, even when an AI tool drafted a method.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would own the fix if the report prescribes the method.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever drafted it, the recommendation is the auditor's, and prescribing a retraining method designs the model fix, which belongs to the model owner and could impair the auditor's objectivity in later audits. The manager has it reworded as the outcome to achieve, such as a cap on missed high-risk cases, leaving the method to the owner. Disclosing the AI drafting tells readers how the text was made; it does not make a design recommendation acceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the method may well work. But choosing how to retrain is the owner's decision; prescribing it puts the auditor in the design role.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI use should be disclosed. But disclosure explains how the text was made; it does not fix a recommendation that designs the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing first seems careful. But it still makes the owner trial the auditor's design instead of choosing their own fix.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps an auditor-designed fix because it seems sound, and D still pushes the auditor's chosen method onto the owner.
Final two: C beats B because disclosing that AI drafted the text changes nothing in it; the recommendation would still design the owner's fix.
Exam cue: AI-drafted report text gets the same review as any draft. Recommendations name the result or control needed; the model owner chooses the technical fix, such as a retraining method.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor Objectivity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.3 Disclosing AI Use and Owning Conclusions (review every AI-drafted statement before it enters a report; recommend the outcome, not a model fix the auditor designed). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A staff assistant opened to customers
questions.question: An Icelandic district-heating utility's generative AI staff assistant, rated low risk in the audit universe, will start answering customers' billing questions with no model change. What should MOST drive the IS audit manager's new rating?

options.A: The novelty of generative AI for the utility's customers
options.B: The assistant's measured accuracy on staff billing questions so far
options.C: Its unchanged model and data since the low staff-use rating
options.D: How likely wrong answers are to harm customers who act on them

questions.key_concept: AI audit universe ratings follow each use; a model reused for a new audience is re-rated by the likelihood and impact of harm to them.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changes in this plan and what stays the same.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risk belongs to a use, not only to a model. The same assistant will now answer customers, who cannot spot a wrong bill explanation the way staff can and may pay or dispute on the strength of it, so the rating follows how likely and how harmful its errors are for them. Accuracy measured on staff questions comes from a different audience asking different questions, so it cannot set the new rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because customers are new to such tools. But novelty is not risk; ratings follow the likelihood and impact of harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is measured evidence. But it comes from staff, who can spot errors; customers ask differently and act on the answers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because nothing technical changed. But risk attaches to the use: a new audience changes who is harmed and how.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks by novelty, which is not risk, and C carries over a rating set for a different audience.
Final two: D beats B because accuracy on staff questions says little about harm to customers, who ask differently and act on the answers.
Exam cue: a new audience is a new AI use. Re-rate it by how likely and how harmful its errors are for the people now relying on it.

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Scores outliving a retired model
questions.question: A Croatian motorway operator retired its bridge-corrosion model in March, yet its last scores still set each bridge's inspection interval. How should the IS audit manager BEST treat it in the AI audit universe?

options.A: Remove it, since a retired model no longer runs or retrains
options.B: Keep it, rated low risk because its stored scores no longer change
options.C: Keep it, ranked by the decisions its stored scores drive today
options.D: Move it to next year, once the decommissioning review is complete

questions.key_concept: AI stays in the audit universe while its outputs drive decisions; stored predictions go stale as conditions change, even after the model is retired.
questions.pre_read: Read what retirement changed and what it did not.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's risk lasts as long as its outputs drive decisions. Retiring the code did not retire the scores: they still set how often each bridge is inspected, and as bridges age, those frozen scores grow stale, raising the likelihood of missed corrosion. So the use stays in the universe, ranked by that likelihood and the impact of the decisions it drives. Rating it low because the scores never change gets it backwards.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model is switched off. But its stored scores still set inspection intervals, so the use and its risk continue.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing in the model can change now. But frozen predictions about aging bridges grow less accurate each month, so their risk rises rather than falls.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a decommissioning review seems the natural point to judge the model. But the intervals rest on the scores now, so waiting a year leaves a live use unplanned.

tips: Eliminate: A treats retirement as the end of the use, and D defers a use whose outputs drive decisions today.
Final two: C beats B because scores frozen in March grow stale as bridges age; fixed predictions about changing assets raise risk, not lower it.
Exam cue: a retired model whose outputs still drive decisions stays in the audit universe. Rank it by likelihood and impact; frozen outputs grow stale, so likelihood rises.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A model that retrains weekly
questions.question: An IS auditor's scope for a Mongolian cashmere trader's price-forecast model, retrained weekly on new auction data, covers the current version's code, accuracy and access controls. What is the GREATEST scope weakness?

options.A: Checks on each week's new model before its release go untested
options.B: The code review may need a specialist in time-series forecasting libraries
options.C: Accuracy tests may not cover every region the trader buys in
options.D: Access controls cover the model but not its weekly forecast reports

questions.key_concept: A model that retrains is a new model each time; scope covers the retraining and release process, not only the current version.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the planned tests would cover across the whole period.
questions.correct_explanation: A model retrained every week is a new model every week, so testing the current version's code and accuracy covers one of the many weekly versions that produced forecasts during the audit period. Retraining changes the model without any code change, so the scope must cover how each weekly version is built, validated and released. Testing accuracy region by region refines work on one version; it says nothing about the others.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because forecasting code can be specialized. But that is a staffing question for planning, not a gap in what the audit covers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because buying regions differ. But it refines a test of one version, while the weekly retrains that produced the others go unexamined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reports can reveal prices. But report access is minor beside the many weekly model versions the scope never reaches.

tips: Eliminate: B is a staffing question rather than scope, and D adds a minor access point beside the model's weekly changes.
Final two: A beats C because region coverage refines a test of one version; weekly retraining produced many models the scope never reaches.
Exam cue: a retrain is a change even with no code change. Scope an AI audit across every version that ran, through retraining and release.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A layered vendor chain
questions.question: A Laotian microfinance firm's loan-help assistant, from a local vendor, runs on a global provider's foundation model, which is retuned several times a year. Which third-party element is MOST important for the IS auditor's scope?

options.A: The foundation model's training data and safety-tuning methods
options.B: The local vendor's service levels and data-handling terms
options.C: How the firm learns of and retests foundation model updates
options.D: The local vendor's security certificate for its hosting

questions.key_concept: For layered AI supply chains, scope how the organization detects and retests upstream foundation model changes, not internals it cannot see.
questions.pre_read: Trace each party in the chain and what each one controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm cannot inspect the global provider, but it owns its use of the assistant. A foundation model update reaches the firm through the local vendor and can change answers without any change the firm makes, so the scope must test how the firm learns of each update and retests before relying on it. Service levels and data terms matter, but they do not show whether upstream model changes are caught.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the base model shapes every answer. But the firm cannot see those internals; audit what it controls, including its oversight of changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the contract governs the vendor. But service and data terms do not show how upstream model updates are detected and retested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is an attestation. But a hosting certificate covers infrastructure, not how the assistant behaves after a model update.

tips: Eliminate: A asks for internals the firm cannot obtain, and D offers a hosting certificate that says nothing about model behavior.
Final two: C beats B because contract terms with the local vendor do not show whether updates to the underlying model are caught and retested.
Exam cue: with layered AI vendors, scope what the organization controls: how it learns of upstream model changes and retests before relying on them.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's jailbreak tests
questions.question: IS audit's independent specialist found all 500 jailbreak attempts on a vendor model's API failed; a Tanzanian mobile bank's assistant app adds a system prompt to that model. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the vendor to confirm the API model matches the app's model
options.B: Have the specialist rerun the tests through the bank's own app
options.C: Rely on the result, since the bank's app calls the vendor model
options.D: Rely on the result, since the specialist is independent and qualified

questions.key_concept: Judge a specialist's AI test against the system as deployed; bare model API results do not carry over to the app wrapping it.
questions.pre_read: Read the test conditions as closely as the result.
questions.correct_explanation: Using an expert's work means judging whether the method fits the objective. The bank's app adds its own system prompt, and may add data or tools, each of which can change how the model responds, so an attack the bare model refuses can succeed through the app. Rerunning the tests through the app checks the assistant customers use. Sharing one underlying model does not carry API results over.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor's confirmation is a claim, and the same model can behave differently inside the app.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model is the same. But the app adds its own prompt and may add data or tools, which can change how attacks land.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the specialist is vetted and independent. But objectivity and skill do not extend tests to a channel never tried.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps a test for the vendor's assurance, and D weighs who ran the tests instead of what they covered.
Final two: B beats C because the app's own system prompt, and any data or tools it adds, can change how the model responds; API results do not carry over to the deployed assistant.
Exam cue: before relying on an AI specialist's result, check that the tests hit the system as deployed: channel, prompts, data, users and version.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1206 (Using the Work of Other Experts); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)

Review round 1, 5 Nov 2026: re-angled from an English-only test of a bilingual assistant (aaia_d2_122's frame) to tests sent to the bare model API instead of the deployed app. Final review, 5 Nov 2026: tip 2 now hedges the app's data and tools as the explanations do. questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's fairness measure
questions.question: The IS auditor's specialist calls a Namibian housing lender's credit model fair because approval rates match across regions; policy requires creditworthy applicants to be refused equally often everywhere. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the conclusion, since matching approval rates meet the policy
options.B: Report the model as fair across regions, naming the measure used
options.C: Ask the model owner which fairness measure the audit should apply
options.D: Have wrongful decline rates by region measured against the policy

questions.key_concept: A specialist's fairness result supports the audit only when it measures what the policy requires; fairness measures can disagree.
questions.pre_read: Check what each fairness figure actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness measures answer different questions and can disagree: approval rates can match across regions while creditworthy applicants in one region are wrongly declined far more often, when regions differ in creditworthiness. The policy is about those wrongful declines, so the specialist's work supports a conclusion only once they are measured by region. Asking the model owner to pick the measure would hand audit criteria to the auditee when the policy already sets them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because matching rates look like equal treatment. But the policy is about wrongful declines, which equal approval rates can hide when regions differ.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it discloses the method. But disclosure does not make approval-rate parity show what the lender's policy requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owners turn fairness into measurable criteria. But the policy already sets the measure, and the IS auditor selects the audit criteria without the auditee's agreement.

tips: Eliminate: A lets approval-rate parity stand in for the policy's test, and B reports a conclusion the measure used cannot support.
Final two: D beats C because the policy already sets the fairness measure; owners set use-level criteria, but the IS auditor selects the audit criteria and needs no auditee agreement.
Exam cue: fairness measures can disagree. Check that a specialist measured what the policy requires before calling a model fair.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An audit agent's system access
questions.question: An audit team's planned AI agent will query a Qatari cold-chain distributor's ERP system for evidence, using a finance service account that can also post entries. What should the chief audit executive require FIRST?

options.A: Read-only access limited to the data the audit needs
options.B: A log of every action the agent takes, reviewed weekly
options.C: A filter that strips instruction-like text from records the agent reads
options.D: A system prompt forbidding the agent to post entries

questions.key_concept: An audit AI agent gets least-privilege, read-only access enforced by the system, so it cannot change the records the audit examines.
questions.pre_read: Consider how the audit's own tools could affect the auditee's records.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent can do anything its account allows, and instructions planted in the records it reads can steer it past its own instructions; filters for such text miss reworded versions. If the agent posted or changed an entry, the audit would alter the very records it tests and could cause errors in the distributor's books. A read-only account scoped to the audit's data enforces the limit in the system, whatever the agent reads.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it records what happened. But weekly review comes after an entry is posted; it detects changes to auditee data rather than preventing them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it blocks planted instructions. But filters miss reworded text, and the agent could still post entries through its own error.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets posting directly. But a prompt is an instruction, not a control; planted text can override it, and the account still allows posting.

tips: Eliminate: B finds unwanted postings only after they happen, and C screens planted text but leaves the account able to post entries.
Final two: A beats D because a prompt is an instruction the agent can be steered past; read-only access blocks posting whatever the agent reads.
Exam cue: give audit AI agents the narrowest system-enforced access. Filters and prompts can be bypassed, and audit tools must not alter auditee data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A.4 Planning the Audit's Own Use of AI (weigh each proposed audit use of AI against its risks and set its limits before any engagement relies on it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A downloaded open-weight model
questions.question: A Kyrgyz gold miner's senior IS auditor wants to analyze confidential logs on an audit laptop using an open-weight model downloaded from a public hub. What should the IS audit manager do FIRST?

options.A: Allow it, since the confidential logs stay on the audit laptop
options.B: Have the tool's origin and file integrity assessed
options.C: Require the auditor to save prompts and outputs in the work papers
options.D: Compare its results with an approved cloud tool on the same logs

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's supply chain is part of its approval: a downloaded model is assessed for source and integrity before audit use.
questions.pre_read: List the risks this tool brings into the audit environment.
questions.correct_explanation: Keeping data on the laptop addresses one risk, confidentiality, but the use is still unapproved. Model files from public hubs can carry malicious code that runs when loaded, or hidden behaviors from tampered weights, and an unvetted model has not been shown to analyze logs reliably. The manager has the model's origin and integrity assessed before approving its audit use, so no engagement relies on it unchecked. Local processing cannot make an untrusted model safe.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the logs stay on the device. But a tampered model file can run malicious code locally, and nobody has approved the use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because records support review. But documenting the use of an unvetted, unapproved model does not make it safe or reliable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because comparison looks like validation. But running the model to compare loads the unchecked file, which is when malicious code would run.

tips: Eliminate: C documents a use nobody approved, and D runs the unchecked file before anyone knows it is safe.
Final two: B beats A because local processing solves confidentiality only; a model from a public hub can carry malicious code or tampered behavior.
Exam cue: approve audit AI tools on more than data location. A downloaded model is outside software: check its origin and integrity first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.2 (Supply Chain Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0010 (AI Supply Chain Compromise)
