questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Design of a fairness alert
questions.question: A Costa Rican arts council's fairness control alerts when its grant-screening model's overall rejection rate moves more than 3 percentage points from last year's. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion about this control's design?

options.A: Its 3-point limit may be too wide to catch meaningful changes
options.B: It needs operating evidence for the period before design is judged
options.C: It cannot detect a gap between groups if the total stays level
options.D: It is sound, since it compares results with a historical baseline

questions.key_concept: A fairness control must measure outcomes by group; an overall rate can hold steady while one group is harmed.
questions.pre_read: Walk the control through the risk it is meant to catch.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness risk is about differences between groups, and an overall rejection rate can stay steady while one group's rejections rise and another's fall. Walking the control through that risk shows it cannot see the harm it exists to catch, so the design is deficient whatever its limit. Tightening the limit would still watch only the overall rate, so it would not remove the blind spot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because limits matter. But any limit on the overall rate still misses group gaps; the flaw is what is measured, not how tightly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because operation needs testing. But design is judged first; a control that cannot see group gaps fails before operation matters.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because baselines catch change. But last year's overall rate says nothing about how this year's groups compare.

tips: Eliminate: B reverses the order of design and operation testing, and D accepts a baseline that measures the wrong thing.
Final two: C beats A because a tighter limit on the overall rate still cannot see one group's rejections rising while another's fall.
Exam cue: test an AI control's design against the specific risk. Fairness controls must measure by group; totals can hide harm.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. A drift monitor that watches inputs
questions.question: An Ethiopian flower exporter's freight-demand model has its tolerance set on forecast error, but its drift monitor watches only inputs and has not alerted in a year. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the year without alerts as evidence the model stayed accurate
options.B: Confirm the input monitor ran on every day of the year
options.C: Obtain the model owner's statement that forecast error stayed within tolerance
options.D: Recompute recent forecast error and compare it with the tolerance

questions.key_concept: Input-drift monitoring does not measure performance; test the metric the tolerance names, since relationships can change while inputs look stable.
questions.pre_read: Read a monitor's design before trusting its record.
questions.correct_explanation: The tolerance is set on forecast error, but the monitor watches only inputs. Inputs can look stable while the link between them and freight demand changes, for example when airlines change schedules, so error can breach the tolerance with no alert. The auditor first recomputes recent forecast error against the tolerance. Confirming that the input monitor ran daily tests the operation of a check that does not measure what the tolerance protects.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the monitor never alerted. But it watches inputs; error can rise while inputs look stable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because operation over the period is standard. But a daily check on inputs still cannot show forecast error met the tolerance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the owner knows the model. But a statement is an assertion; only recomputed forecast error shows the tolerance was met.

tips: Eliminate: A reads silence from an input monitor as proof of accuracy, and C rests on the owner's assertion instead of evidence.
Final two: D beats B because daily operation of an input monitor cannot show forecast error stayed within tolerance; only recomputed error can.
Exam cue: match the monitor to the tolerance. Input drift checks can stay quiet while performance falls, so measure the metric the tolerance names.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Sampling unit for an agent
questions.question: An IS auditor will sample a Dominican resort group's AI agent, which onboards each new supplier through 10 to 30 tool calls, such as sanctions checks and bank-detail updates. Which sampling unit is BEST?

options.A: Whole supplier onboardings, tracing every tool call within each
options.B: Supplier records the agent itself marked as successfully onboarded
options.C: Individual tool calls drawn at random from the agent's call log
options.D: Onboardings the sanctions check flagged, with their final records

questions.key_concept: For an AI agent, sample whole tasks and trace every step, because errors arise in the order and gaps between tool calls.
questions.pre_read: Decide what a single decision is for this system before choosing what to sample.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's control risks sit in the sequence: whether the sanctions check ran before bank details changed, or whether a step was skipped. A sample of whole onboardings lets the auditor trace each one end to end and judge it as one decision. Tool calls drawn at random each look normal on their own and cannot show order, omissions or how one step's result shaped the next.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because these are completed cases. But the agent marked them itself, so failures it judged as successes stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because calls are what the log records. But single calls lose their context; skipped or out-of-order steps show only in the whole task.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because flagged cases seem riskiest. But onboardings the check cleared, where errors go unnoticed, are left out.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the agent's own success marks define the population, and D keeps only cases the sanctions check flagged.
Final two: A beats C because random calls each look normal alone; only a whole onboarding shows a skipped check or steps in the wrong order.
Exam cue: sample an AI agent by task, not by tool call. Its errors live in sequence, omissions and how one step feeds the next.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF Guideline 2208 (Information Technology Audit Sampling); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.2 Sampling AI Decisions (design an AI sample around where errors hide, and document the design and its reasons). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Scoring answers that vary between runs
questions.question: Testing a Georgian wine-export agency's chatbot against current labeling rules, an IS auditor asks each of 40 questions five times; one question gets a wrong answer once. How should the auditor BEST treat that question?

options.A: As a pass, since four of its five answers were correct
options.B: As an exception, since exporters can receive the wrong answer
options.C: As a pass, unless the wrong answer recurs on further asking
options.D: As untested, until the chatbot's vendor explains why answers vary

questions.key_concept: Generative AI answers vary run to run; a wrong answer in any run is an exception, because users can receive it.
questions.pre_read: Decide what one test result means when the same input can give different outputs.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the chatbot generates each reply with some randomness, one question has a range of possible answers, and any exporter may get the wrong one. A wrong answer in one of five runs is an error the chatbot actually gives, so the question is an exception, and the runs help estimate how often it happens. Treating four correct answers as a pass takes the majority as the chatbot's answer, but exporters receive every variant.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because most answers were right. But exporters get whichever answer is generated; a wrong one in five still reaches some of them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one wrong answer can look like a fluke. But varying output may not repeat on demand; the wrong answer was still given.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the variation needs explaining. But the auditor already has a test result; the vendor's account does not change what exporters received.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for an error that may not repeat on demand, and D sets aside a result the auditor already has.
Final two: B beats A because exporters receive every variant; four correct answers in five still leave a wrong one reaching some exporters.
Exam cue: when a model's answers vary, every run is a test item. A wrong answer in any run is an exception, not noise outvoted by the majority.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Rule query or anomaly tool
questions.question: An IS auditor can test all 120,000 credit limits a Serbian lender's model set this year; policy caps each at three times monthly income, and the audit's anomaly tool is validated. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Test a statistical sample of 60 limits against the policy cap
options.B: Run the validated anomaly tool over the limits and test its flags
options.C: Review the model's validation report for how often it breached the cap
options.D: Run a query comparing every limit with the policy cap

questions.key_concept: When a policy gives an exact rule, a full-population query tests it completely; anomaly detection finds the unusual, not every breach.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the policy lets you test exactly.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy gives an exact rule, so a query can test every limit against it and list each breach. An anomaly tool, however well validated, flags what looks unusual compared with the rest; if the model breaches the cap often, breaches look normal and go unflagged, and its misses stay untested. AI analytics suit patterns no rule can state, not a test a simple rule performs completely.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sampling is standard. But every limit can be tested against an exact rule, which a sample of 60 cannot match.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the tool is validated and covers every limit. But anomaly tools flag rarity; frequent breaches look normal, and unflagged limits stay untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because builders test their models. But pre-release validation does not show this year's production limits met the cap.

tips: Eliminate: A samples where every item can be checked against an exact rule, and C relies on builders' testing before release.
Final two: D beats B because an anomaly tool flags what is rare; if breaches are common they look normal, so a rule query is the complete test.
Exam cue: use simple rules for full-population tests of exact criteria. Keep AI analytics for patterns rules cannot express; unflagged is not tested.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. A fairness dashboard's figures
questions.question: A Colombian bank's fairness dashboard compares approval rates by sex using only completed applications; its model asks some applicants for extra documents, and many then withdraw. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the dashboard, since the bank's own systems generate it
options.B: Recompute approval rates by sex from completed applications in the logs
options.C: Recompute approval rates by sex from all applications, withdrawals included
options.D: Ask the model owner why applicants withdraw after document requests

questions.key_concept: When a model's own actions remove people before the decision, fairness is measured on everyone who applied, not only completed cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the metric's population leaves out, and why.
questions.correct_explanation: The model does more than approve or decline: its document requests drive withdrawals, so a measure built on completed applications leaves out people the model effectively turned away. If requests fall more on one sex, the dashboard can look fair while the process is not. Recomputing from all applications, withdrawals included, tests the model's whole effect. Reperforming the dashboard's figures only confirms its arithmetic on the same narrowed population.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the figures are system-generated. But the system applies a definition that leaves out applicants the model's requests drove away.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it repeats the dashboard's definition, so withdrawals the model caused stay outside the measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seeks the cause. But inquiry comes after evidence; first measure whether withdrawals differ by sex.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a system's figures without checking what they measure, and D asks for explanations before the evidence is in.
Final two: C beats B because reperforming the dashboard repeats its narrowed population; only all applications show whether document requests drove one sex away.
Exam cue: check how a fairness metric's population was formed. If the model's actions remove people early, recompute from everyone who applied.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Reading a retrieval log
questions.question: An Estonian e-government assistant gave a resident the wrong benefit deadline; its retrieval log holds the text of the one passage it was given, stating the correct deadline. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The error arose as the model wrote its answer from that passage
options.B: The guidance library held an outdated deadline for that benefit
options.C: The cause stays open until the passage's version history is checked
options.D: The resident's question was too vague for a reliable answer

questions.key_concept: When a retrieval log shows the right passage reached the model, a wrong answer points to generation, not the source library.
questions.pre_read: Before the options, ask what the stated record already rules in or out.
questions.correct_explanation: The retrieval log holds the text the assistant was given: one passage, stating the correct deadline, so source and retrieval were right and the error arose as the model wrote its answer; models can misstate even a correct passage. Checking the passage's version history, option C, suits a log that records only a passage ID, but this log holds the text supplied, so the history cannot change this conclusion.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wrong answers often trace to outdated sources. But the log shows the passage supplied held the correct deadline.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because corroborating a record is careful practice. But the log holds the exact text supplied, and it was correct, so the history adds nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vague questions draw weak answers. But nothing in the stem says the question was unclear, and the right passage was found.

tips: Eliminate: B blames the library, which the log shows was correct, and D assumes a vague question the stem never describes.
Final two: A beats C because the log holds the exact passage text supplied, and it was right; the version history adds nothing about this answer.
Exam cue: compare a retrieval assistant's answer with the passages it was given. Right passage and wrong answer means generation failed; wrong passage means the source or retrieval did.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Support for a model card's claim
questions.question: A Paraguayan job-matching platform's model card states that its ranking model, retrained monthly, was tested for bias across age groups. Which evidence BEST supports this statement for the IS auditor?

options.A: The age-group fairness report from the model's first release
options.B: This version's fairness test results by age group
options.C: The datasheet showing the age mix of this version's training data
options.D: The policy requiring age-group bias tests before each release

questions.key_concept: A model card's claims are the builders' description; the underlying test report, by group and version, is the evidence.
questions.pre_read: Rank the evidence by how directly it shows the claim.
questions.correct_explanation: A model card is the builders' own description, so a claim in it needs the record it summarizes: the fairness test report, with results by age group, for the version now ranking candidates, since monthly retraining replaces earlier versions. The datasheet's age mix shows what the model learned from, not how it ranks older and younger job seekers; a balanced dataset can still produce unequal rankings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is a real fairness test by age. But monthly retraining has replaced that model; the claim must hold for the version now ranking candidates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because balanced data seems to imply fair results. But training composition shows inputs, not how the model ranks each age group.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it requires testing. But a policy shows intent, not that this version was tested or passed.

tips: Eliminate: A tests a version monthly retraining has replaced, and D shows a requirement, not that it was met.
Final two: B beats C because the training data's age mix shows what the model learned from, not how it ranks each age group.
Exam cue: to support a model card's claim, get the record it summarizes. Data composition is not a test result.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Preserving a continuously learning model
questions.question: A Bahraini Islamic bank's fraud model updates its weights continuously from each confirmed case. Which preservation request BEST lets the IS auditor later rerun the model on decisions from the audit period?

options.A: The training code and the dataset that built the model's first version
options.B: A full copy of the updated model as it stands at fieldwork
options.C: The decision log of each transaction's score and outcome
options.D: Regular snapshots of the model, with the update data between them

questions.key_concept: A continuously learning model has no fixed version; reperforming past decisions needs periodic snapshots and the update data between them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a later rerun would need to recreate.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that learns from every confirmed case is a slightly different model after each update, so one copy taken at fieldwork reproduces only today's decisions. Regular snapshots, with the confirmed cases applied between them, let the auditor rebuild the model as it stood when a past decision was made, or come close, and rerun it. Decision logs record what was decided, but cannot show the model then in force would decide that way.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it shows how the model began. But thousands of updates have shaped it since; the starting point cannot reproduce later states.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it preserves the model before further change. But it captures only today's state; earlier decisions came from states the updates have replaced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs are strong evidence of what happened. But they record results; rerunning needs the model state that produced them.

tips: Eliminate: A preserves only the starting point of a model that has changed since, and C records results without the model that produced them.
Final two: D beats B because a continuously learning model changes with each case; one copy at fieldwork cannot rerun decisions made months earlier.
Exam cue: a model that keeps learning has no single version. Preserve regular snapshots and the update data between them to rerun past decisions.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Model-written review reasons
questions.question: A Lebanese retailer's warranty assessors must give reasons for accepting the model's claim rejections; the screen pre-fills model-written reasons, which most keep. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern with these reasons as evidence?

options.A: They may be too short to explain each rejection fully
options.B: The model-written reasons may contain factual errors about the claims
options.C: They may record the model's text, not any human judgment
options.D: They may not be kept for the whole audit period

questions.key_concept: A pre-filled, model-written reason that reviewers keep evidences the model's text, not human review, and invites automation bias.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each record would look like if no real review took place.
questions.correct_explanation: The reasons field is meant to evidence each assessor's review, but when the screen supplies a model-written reason and most assessors keep it, the field records the model's text, not human judgment. Pre-filled answers also anchor reviewers toward agreement, so the records may reflect automation bias rather than review. The auditor needs other evidence, such as review times, overrides or seeded cases. Errors in the reasons matter, but they do not show whether review happened.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because brief reasons explain little. But length is not the problem; who wrote the reason is.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generated text can be wrong. But the question is whether the field shows review; even accurate text would be the model's, not the assessor's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retention limits evidence. But nothing suggests a retention gap; the reasons' authorship is the issue.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about length when authorship is at issue, and D raises a retention gap nothing suggests.
Final two: C beats B because even accurate model text, kept unchanged, shows acceptance, not the assessor's judgment.
Exam cue: evidence of human review must come from the human. Pre-filled AI text that reviewers keep signals automation bias, not oversight.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An AI tool's account of its own ratings
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI tool rated 400 of an Armenian mining company's quarterly access reviews adequate and, when asked, gave a confident rationale for each rating. How should the auditor BEST treat the rationales?

options.A: As leads, checking a sample of ratings against review records
options.B: As evidence, since each rationale cites the review's own content
options.C: As documentation of the tool's method, filed with each rating
options.D: As evidence, since each rationale reads as clear and convincing

questions.key_concept: An AI tool's explanation of its own output is generated text, not a record of its method; verify the output against source records.
questions.pre_read: Separate records of work done from descriptions of it.
questions.correct_explanation: A rationale written on request is new generated text, not a record of how the tool reached its rating; it can sound convincing and still be wrong, or describe reasoning the tool never used. So the ratings and their rationales stay leads until the auditor checks a sample against the access review records. Filing the rationales as the tool's method would document a story about the work, not the work itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because quotes look grounded. But citing a review does not show the rating is right; quotes can be wrong or invented.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because method should be documented. But a generated explanation is not a trace of how a rating was made; method comes from version, prompt and inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the reasoning reads well. But fluent, confident text is what such tools produce whether right or wrong; only source records show accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: B takes quotation as proof, and D takes persuasiveness as proof; neither shows a rating is right.
Final two: A beats C because a rationale generated on request is not a trace of the tool's method; the ratings still need checking against records.
Exam cue: an AI's explanation of itself is more output, not evidence. Corroborate the result with source records.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A finding resting on an AI code explanation
questions.question: A draft finding against an Indonesian nickel smelter rests on one line of a production access script that an approved AI tool says grants all users admin rights. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask a second approved AI tool to explain the line and compare
options.B: Check the permissions the script has set in the live system
options.C: Ask the smelter's script author to confirm the tool's explanation
options.D: Rely on the explanation, since the tool is approved for audit work

questions.key_concept: An AI tool's explanation of code is a lead; a finding that rests on it needs the effect confirmed in the system.
questions.pre_read: Ask how much of the finding depends on this one piece of evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: A finding resting on one line stands or falls on what that line does, and AI explanations of code can be fluent and wrong, for example by misreading a condition or an exception. Checking the permissions the script actually set in the live system gives evidence of its effect. Approval lets auditors use the tool; it does not verify each output, least of all one a finding depends on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a second tool looks independent. But two models can share a misreading, and neither shows what the script actually set.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the author knows the script. But the auditee has an interest in the reading; the system's actual settings are independent evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool passed approval. But approval permits use; it does not make each output reliable, especially one a finding rests on.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps one model's reading for another's, and C asks the party with an interest in the reading to confirm it.
Final two: B beats D because approval lets the team use the tool; it does not verify an explanation a finding depends on.
Exam cue: when a conclusion rests on AI-processed evidence, confirm that evidence independently. Tool approval is not verification of each output.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A synthetic copy of a decision log
questions.question: Testing which batches a Greek olive-oil exporter's supplier-risk model sent for lab tests, an IS auditor is offered a synthetic log matching the real log's statistics, to protect growers' data. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Rare, high-risk batches may be smoothed out of the copy
options.B: Growers might still be re-identified from the synthetic records
options.C: The data team, not the auditor, generated the synthetic log
options.D: Its records show no selection that actually took place

questions.key_concept: Testing AI decisions needs records of what happened; synthetic data built to match statistics shows no real decision, however faithful.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each record in the offered log came to be.
questions.correct_explanation: A synthetic log is generated to resemble the real one, so none of its records is a choice the supplier-risk model actually made. Tests on it can show patterns, but not whether any real batch was scored, sent for testing or passed over. The auditor needs the real log, with protections such as masked grower names. Losing rare batches is a real weakness, but even a perfect copy would hold no real choices.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because synthetic data often loses rare cases. But even a copy that kept every rare pattern would describe invented batches, not real choices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because synthetic records can leak personal data. But that is a privacy risk for the exporter; for the audit, no record shows a real choice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditee-prepared data needs checking. But a synthetic log the auditor generated would still show no choice the model made.

tips: Eliminate: B is the exporter's privacy risk, not a flaw in the evidence, and C asks who made the copy, which cannot make it real.
Final two: D beats A because even a synthetic log that kept every rare batch would describe invented cases, not choices the model made.
Exam cue: synthetic data can help test a tool but cannot show what an AI system did. Tests of AI decisions need the real records, protected if needed.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A model-inferred attribute in test data
questions.question: For a fairness test of a Spanish gym chain's membership-pricing model, the data team supplies members' sex inferred from names by another model. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern in relying on this data?

options.A: The pricing model may use members' names as an input
options.B: Inferring members' sex may breach the gym chain's data-minimization rules
options.C: Inference errors may differ by name origin and distort the comparison
options.D: The name model's vendor terms may not allow this use

questions.key_concept: Attributes inferred by a model are outputs with group-varying errors; validate them before relying on them in audit tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask where each field in the audit data came from and how it was produced.
questions.correct_explanation: The group label driving the test is itself a model's guess. Name-based inference errs more for some names, such as unisex names or names from less common origins, so members can be counted in the wrong group unevenly, masking or inventing a gap. The auditor needs the inference's error rate by group, or a verified sample, before relying on the comparison. Privacy rules matter, but they do not decide whether the result is right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because names can act as proxies. But that concerns the pricing model's inputs; the question is whether the test data's sex labels are reliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because inferring sex touches personal data. But even a permitted use would rest on guessed labels; reliance turns on whether they are right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because license terms matter. But nothing suggests a breach, and terms do not affect whether the labels are accurate.

tips: Eliminate: A shifts to the pricing model's inputs, and D raises license terms with nothing suggesting a breach.
Final two: C beats B because even a permitted use would rest on guessed labels; uneven inference errors can hide or invent the gap being tested.
Exam cue: when a model inferred the group labels in fairness test data, check its error rate by group first; uneven label errors can hide or invent the gap.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A prompt reworded after validation
questions.question: A Zambian copper miner's audit team validated its generative AI invoice-matching tool on 5,000 past invoices, then reworded its prompt to cut false alarms on live invoices. What BEST supports relying on it now?

options.A: A rerun of the validation cases with the reworded prompt
options.B: The vendor's published rate for catching invoice mismatches
options.C: The drop in false alarms since the prompt was reworded
options.D: The original validation, since the tool's model is unchanged

questions.key_concept: A generative audit tool's prompt is part of the tool; rewording it after validation means rerunning the known cases before reliance continues.
questions.pre_read: Note what changed after validation and what each option could actually show.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool's prompt is part of the tool: rewording it changes what the model is asked to do, so the validation covered a tool that no longer runs. The rewording came from live invoices, not the validation cases, so rerunning those cases with the new prompt is still a fair test of whether it catches the known mismatches. Relying on the original validation because the model is unchanged ignores the prompt.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it measures mismatches directly. But it comes from the vendor's own data and prompts, not this tool as reworded on the miner's invoices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cutting false alarms was the goal. But fewer flags can mean more missed mismatches; false alarms alone cannot show detection held.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model itself did not change. But the prompt shapes every answer, so a reworded prompt makes the validated tool a different one.

tips: Eliminate: B is the vendor's figure from its own data, and C counts fewer false alarms, which cannot show what the tool now misses.
Final two: A beats D because a generative tool's prompt is part of the tool; with the model unchanged but the prompt reworded, the validated tool no longer runs.
Exam cue: for a generative audit tool, a prompt change is a tool change. Revalidate on known cases before relying on it again.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A split-purchase tool's validation set
questions.question: A Tunisian date exporter's audit team validated its AI split-purchase tool on 300 known split purchases, all found earlier by a prior version of the tool. What is the GREATEST concern with this validation?

options.A: The known splits may span too few years to reflect current buying
options.B: The tool's false-alarm rate may make follow-up work costly
options.C: The prior version's results may differ from the current version's
options.D: The known cases hold only splits of kinds the tool can find

questions.key_concept: Known cases chosen by the tool itself cannot reveal its misses; validation sets need cases found independently of the tool.
questions.pre_read: Check how the validation cases were assembled before reading the score.
questions.correct_explanation: A validation set is only as good as the way its cases were found. Every known split here was found by the same tool, so splits its approach misses, such as orders spread across two buyers or several weeks, cannot be in the set, and the measured detection rate will look high whatever the tool misses. False alarms matter for effort, but they do not make the tool's misses visible.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because buying patterns change. But nothing suggests the period is short; the problem is which splits the set can contain at all.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because false alarms waste effort. But they cost time, while a set the tool selected hides the misses that matter for reliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because versions differ. But the current version was the one tested; the issue is how the cases were chosen.

tips: Eliminate: A doubts the set's time span with nothing suggesting it is short, and C questions a version difference when the current version was the one tested.
Final two: D beats B because false alarms only cost effort; cases the tool chose for itself hide exactly the misses that reliance depends on.
Exam cue: validate an audit AI tool on cases found independently of it. A test set the tool selected measures only what it already finds.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Sharing a loaded assistant
questions.question: A Swiss audit firm's IS auditor built a custom assistant on the firm's approved AI service, loaded it with one client's control documents and shared it firm-wide. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The service vendor may use the client's documents to train its models
options.B: Staff on other engagements can query the client's documents through it
options.C: Its answers may differ when colleagues ask the same question
options.D: Its version and settings may go unrecorded in the work papers

questions.key_concept: Files loaded into a shared AI assistant are retrievable by all its users; access to audit data follows the engagement, not the tool.
questions.pre_read: List every party who can reach the audit data after each step.
questions.correct_explanation: Files loaded into a custom assistant become part of what it can retrieve and quote, so sharing the assistant shares the documents with everyone who can use it, including teams serving other clients. That breaches client confidentiality inside the firm, whatever the vendor's terms. The service is approved, so its terms on training and retention were already assessed; the new exposure is the firm-wide sharing of one client's files.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors may reuse inputs. But the service is approved, so its training terms were assessed; the new exposure is inside the firm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because generated answers vary. But variation affects reproducibility, not who can read the client's documents.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records support review. But a documentation gap is minor beside confidential files open to the whole firm.

tips: Eliminate: C is a reproducibility point and D a record-keeping one; neither touches who can read the client's files.
Final two: B beats A because the approved service's vendor terms were already assessed; sharing the assistant opens one client's files to every team.
Exam cue: anything loaded into an AI assistant can be retrieved by whoever can use it. Limit audit assistants to the engagement team.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Embeddings of work papers
questions.question: A Maltese pension fund's audit team plans to keep embeddings of confidential work papers in an unapproved vendor's vector database, reasoning they are only numbers. What is the chief audit executive's BEST decision?

options.A: Allow it, since embeddings cannot be turned back into readable text
options.B: Remove names from the papers before embedding them
options.C: Apply the work papers' data rules to the embeddings as well
options.D: Require the vendor to encrypt the vector database at rest

questions.key_concept: Embeddings derived from confidential audit data carry its confidentiality; they stay in approved services under the same rules.
questions.pre_read: Check whether a transformed copy still reveals its source.
questions.correct_explanation: Embeddings are derived from the text and keep much of its meaning: published research has reconstructed much of the original wording from them, and similarity searches reveal what the papers discuss. So they carry the work papers' confidentiality and stay inside approved services under the same data rules. Encryption at rest protects stored disks, but the unapproved vendor still holds and processes the data under terms nobody assessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vectors look meaningless. But inversion attacks can reconstruct much of the original text from embeddings.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because names are the obvious identifiers. But findings and context still identify people and issues, and inversion can recover them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption is a standard control. But it guards stored disks; the unapproved vendor still processes the data under unassessed terms.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes embeddings cannot be reversed, and B assumes names are all that identifies people.
Final two: C beats D because encryption at rest protects stored disks; the unapproved vendor still holds and processes data derived from confidential papers.
Exam cue: derived AI data, such as embeddings, inherits the source's confidentiality. Keep it inside approved services under the same rules.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Recommendation on a vendor's silent change
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a Cameroonian bank's vendor-hosted chatbot quoted outdated exchange rates for a month after the vendor changed its data feed without telling the bank. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: The bank's vendor manager should require change notices and retests
options.B: The vendor should restore and retest its exchange-rate data feed
options.C: The bank should pin the chatbot to one fixed model version
options.D: The bank's chatbot team should add a disclaimer that rates may lag

questions.key_concept: Recommendations on vendor AI address the organization's control over every vendor change, with a named internal owner; pinning the model covers only one component.
questions.pre_read: Locate the control gap that let the problem run for a month.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding's cause is the bank's missing control over vendor changes: the vendor changed a feed, and nothing at the bank detected it for a month. The recommendation goes to the bank's management, with an owner who requires notice of vendor changes and retests the chatbot after each one. Pinning the model version sounds like change control, but this change was to a data feed, which a pinned model would still read.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor's change caused the error. But the report recommends to the bank, and fixing one feed leaves the next change undetected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because version pinning is a sound AI control. But this change came through a data feed; a pinned model still reads whatever the feed supplies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns customers. But a disclaimer leaves wrong rates in place and does nothing about changes going unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: B addresses the vendor rather than the bank's control gap, and D warns customers while wrong rates continue.
Final two: A beats C because the change was to a data feed, not the model; only notice and retesting of every vendor change catch it.
Exam cue: an AI system changes through models, data feeds, prompts and settings. Recommend control over every vendor change, not just the model version.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. An agent with clean test results
questions.question: A Fijian kava exporter's AI agent reads growers' messages and can approve crop-payment advances of any amount; the IS auditor found no improper advances, and red-team tests passed. How should the auditor BEST report this?

options.A: Report no finding, since testing found no improper advances
options.B: Report an observation, since testing and red-teaming found no misuse
options.C: Recommend adding an advance limit to the agent's instructions
options.D: Report the uncapped advance authority, with the exposure as its effect

questions.key_concept: An AI agent's uncapped authority is a reportable control gap even before loss; the effect is the exposure it creates.
questions.pre_read: Separate what testing found from what the system allows to happen.
questions.correct_explanation: A missing control is a finding even before it causes loss. The agent reads growers' messages, whose wording can steer it, and nothing in the payment system caps an advance, so one manipulated conversation could cost any amount. The auditor reports the uncapped authority as the condition and the exposure as the effect. Passed red-team tests show only that the attacks tried failed, not that the authority is controlled.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because testing found nothing improper. But clean results show no loss so far, not that the authority is controlled.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sampling and red-teaming both came back clean. But red-team tests sample attacks; an uncapped agent steered by new wording can still approve any amount.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sets a limit. But a limit in instructions can be argued around; the cap must be enforced by the payment system.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a clean sample as proof of control, and C puts the limit in instructions the agent can be talked out of.
Final two: D beats B because passed red-team tests sample attacks, they do not cap them; an agent growers can steer, with no cap, is an exposure now.
Exam cue: report missing AI limits as findings when the exposure is real, even with no loss yet. The effect can be the exposure itself.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. One model error in two uses
questions.question: Two teams at an Ivorian utility use one sentiment model with a 12% error rate: one ranks call-backs for call-center staff, the other closes complaints automatically. How should the IS auditor BEST rate the findings?

options.A: Rate the call-back findings higher, as staff act on them daily
options.B: Rate automatic closing higher, as no person checks its errors
options.C: Rate both findings equally, as one model and one error rate apply
options.D: Rate both low, as 12% error is typical for sentiment models

questions.key_concept: The same AI flaw is rated by the likelihood and impact of harm in each use; autonomy without human review raises the rating.
questions.pre_read: Compare what happens to an error in each use.
questions.correct_explanation: Findings are rated by the likelihood and impact of harm, not by the technical flaw alone. The same 12% error rate does different damage in each use: a wrong call-back suggestion reaches staff who can still judge the call, while a wrong automatic closure ends a customer's complaint with no person in the loop. So the closing use is rated higher. Rating both equally because the model matches treats technical severity as the rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because staff use the suggestions daily. But staff can catch a wrong suggestion; a wrongly closed complaint reaches the customer unchecked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model and its errors are identical. But ratings follow harm in each use, and only one use acts without a person checking.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the rate may be normal for such models. But a typical error rate can still cause harm a use cannot tolerate.

tips: Eliminate: A counts use without asking who can catch errors, and D rates against an industry norm rather than harm.
Final two: B beats C because identical technical flaws carry different harm: one use keeps a person in the loop, the other acts on customers directly.
Exam cue: rate AI findings by harm in each use. The same model error is worse where it acts without human review.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.2 (Treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and resources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.2 Rating, Reporting and Follow-Up of AI Findings (rate findings by the likelihood and impact of harm, weighing autonomy, scale and whether affected people can appeal). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Retesting a retrained model
questions.question: At follow-up, an Azerbaijani marketplace's fake-review model, retrained on the 20 fakes it missed in the IS auditor's test, now flags all 20. Which test BEST supports closing the finding?

options.A: Rerun the 20 missed fake reviews to confirm they are now flagged
options.B: Review the data science team's report on the retrained model's accuracy
options.C: Test recent fake reviews the retrained model never saw in training
options.D: Accept management's demonstration of the 20 newly flagged reviews

questions.key_concept: AI follow-up tests unseen cases; a model retrained on the reported failures can pass them by memory alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a passing result would prove, and what it would not.
questions.correct_explanation: Once the 20 missed fakes were added to training, the retrained model has learned those exact cases, so flagging them shows memory, not detection. Rerunning them proves only that they were absorbed. Recent fake reviews the model never saw in training test whether it now detects the kinds of fakes it missed, which is what closing the finding requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because these are the reported misses. But the model trained on them; flagging cases it has learned shows memory, not a fixed cause.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it covers the retrained version. But builders' testing is not the auditor's evidence and may include the same 20 cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the demonstration looks convincing. But management chose what to show; closure needs the auditor's own testing.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the builders' own report, and D closes on a demonstration management chose.
Final two: C beats A because the model was trained on the 20 misses; only unseen fake reviews show whether detection improved.
Exam cue: when a model is retrained on the cases an audit reported, retest on cases it never saw. Known failures can be memorized without curing the cause.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. A vendor's warranty in audit reports
questions.question: A Malawian tea estate's chief audit executive plans to state in audit reports that the AI testing tool's vendor warrants its benchmark accuracy. What is the IS audit manager's BEST advice?

options.A: Replace it with how the tool was applied and what auditors verified
options.B: Keep the statement and add the vendor's published accuracy rate
options.C: Keep the statement, as it tells readers who stands behind the tool
options.D: Remove the statement, as reports do not usually name audit tools

questions.key_concept: Disclosure of AI in the audit describes use and verification; a vendor's warranty never moves accountability for audit conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Read each proposed sentence as the audit committee would.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit function owns every conclusion in its reports, whatever tools helped. A vendor's warranty is a commercial promise to the buyer, measured on the vendor's own benchmark rather than this audit's data; quoting it suggests the vendor stands behind the audit's results, which it does not. Readers need how the tool was used and what the auditors verified themselves, which is what disclosing AI use is for.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because figures look objective. But a vendor's accuracy rate comes from its own data, not this audit, and adds a claim, not assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems open about the tool. But it implies the vendor answers for audit conclusions, which stay with the audit function.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit reports rarely name their software. But material use of AI in the audit should be disclosed, with what the auditors verified.

tips: Eliminate: B adds the vendor's own figure as if it were assurance, and D treats AI like other audit software and drops the disclosure of its use.
Final two: A beats C because a vendor's warranty does not make the vendor answerable for audit conclusions; readers need what the auditors did and checked.
Exam cue: disclose how AI was used and what you verified. Never present a vendor's promise as support for audit conclusions.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1005 (Due Professional Care)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.3 Disclosing AI Use and Owning Conclusions (disclose material use of AI in the audit; disclosure never moves accountability to the tool). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Supervising an AI-assisted work paper
questions.question: A Bangladeshi exporter's IS audit manager finds a work paper concluding, from an approved AI tool alone, that all 650 supplier bank-detail changes had callbacks. Which step BEST supports the conclusion before sign-off?

options.A: Rerun the tool on the same records to confirm its conclusion
options.B: Have the preparer verify a sample against the underlying source records
options.C: Sign off, since the tool is approved for audit testing
options.D: Check the tool's validation record before signing off the work paper

questions.key_concept: Supervising AI-assisted work, the reviewer needs evidence of what the auditor verified; tool approval or validation does not stand in for it.
questions.pre_read: Read the work paper as a reviewer who must sign it.
questions.correct_explanation: Supervision asks whether each conclusion rests on sufficient evidence the auditor checked. Here the work paper holds only the tool's output: nothing shows whether all 650 changes were in its input or whether any callback was confirmed. Having the preparer verify a sample against change and callback records, and document it, gives the conclusion evidence. The tool's validation shows it worked on test cases, not that this run was complete and right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a rerun seems to confirm. But repeating the same tool on the same data checks consistency, not accuracy or completeness.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because approval sounds like assurance. But approval permits use; each conclusion still needs the auditor's own checks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because validation supports reliance. But it shows the tool worked on test cases, not that this run's inputs and results were right.

tips: Eliminate: A checks the tool against itself, and C treats approval of the tool as proof of this result.
Final two: B beats D because validation shows the tool can work, not that this run covered all 650 changes and got them right.
Exam cue: an AI tool's output in a work paper is unfinished work. Supervisors look for the auditor's own checks against source records.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1204 (Performance and Supervision); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A model that feeds other models
questions.question: A Mozambican mobile operator's IS audit plan covers its credit-limit and bundle-pricing models but not its churn model, whose scores both use as inputs. What is the IS audit manager's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Drift or bias in the scores would reach the two models unexamined
options.B: The score feed's interface controls between the models are untested
options.C: The churn model uses a more advanced method than the other two
options.D: Bundle prices are a commercial matter, so their audit wastes effort

questions.key_concept: A model whose scores feed other models carries its errors into their decisions; audits of the receiving models usually take those scores as given.
questions.pre_read: Note what the plan includes and excludes before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The churn model's scores are inputs to credit limits and bundle prices, so its drift or bias becomes decisions about customers through both models. Audits of those models usually test how they use the score, not whether it is right. Interface controls matter, but they show only that scores arrive intact; a drifting score arrives intact and still misleads both models.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data passed between systems needs interface controls. But those show scores arrive intact, not that they are right; a drifting score still passes them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complex models seem riskier. But audit priority follows the likelihood and impact of harm, not the method.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pricing seems a commercial matter. But bundle prices land on customers, so that model's harm to people counts toward its priority.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks by technical novelty, and D overlooks that bundle prices land on customers, so that model's harm to people counts too.
Final two: A beats B because interface controls show scores arrive intact, not that they are right; only auditing the churn model tests its own drift and bias.
Exam cue: a model whose outputs feed other models carries its risk into every decision they make. Audits of the receiving models usually take those outputs as given.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An advisory model in the plan
questions.question: A Queensland child-safety agency's audit universe rates its hotline-screening model low risk because caseworkers decide each visit; they accept 98% of its recommendations, most within seconds. What is the GREATEST weakness in this rating?

options.A: It ignores how advanced the model's machine-learning method is
options.B: It does not show caseworkers are trained and authorized to override
options.C: It credits a caseworker review that rarely changes the outcome
options.D: It should rest on the model's accuracy at launch, not on caseworkers

questions.key_concept: A human step lowers AI risk only if it changes outcomes; fast, near-total agreement means a rating cannot credit the review untested.
questions.pre_read: Compare the rating's reasoning with how decisions are really made.
questions.correct_explanation: A human in the loop lowers risk only if the human changes outcomes. Caseworkers accepting 98% of recommendations within seconds suggests automation bias: the model largely decides which reports get a visit, so its errors become decisions about children's safety. Rating the use low because people decide credits a review that rarely acts. Training and authority to override, even if shown, would not prove the review catches errors.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because complex methods seem riskier. But novelty is not risk; ratings follow the likelihood and impact of harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because trained, authorized reviewers are a real control. But 98% agreement in seconds suggests the review rarely changes outcomes, so paper authority cannot justify a low rating.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accuracy matters. But launch accuracy says nothing about harm when errors are followed, and the weakness here is crediting a review that rarely acts.

tips: Eliminate: A rates by technical novelty, and D rests the rating on launch accuracy.
Final two: C beats B because override authority on paper does not show the review changes outcomes; 98% agreement in seconds points to automation bias.
Exam cue: when reviewers agree with a model almost always and fast, rate the use as if the model decides, then test the review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Risk Assessment in Planning)

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A scam model retrained monthly
questions.question: A Finnish dating service retrains its scam-profile model monthly on moderators' verdicts, and moderators review only the profiles the model flags. Which area is MOST important for the IS auditor to bring into scope?

options.A: Accuracy reported separately for each kind of scam and in total
options.B: How the labels that each retrain learns from are produced
options.C: Backup and recovery of the retraining environment
options.D: Specialist review of the model's neural network architecture

questions.key_concept: A model retrained on outcomes it selected never learns what it misses; scope covers how its labels are produced, not only its accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Follow the model through one monthly cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: Moderators see only what the model flags, so every label it retrains on comes from its own choices. Scam profiles it misses are never reviewed, never labeled and never learned, and the blind spot can widen with each monthly retrain. Scope must cover how labels are produced. Accuracy by scam type is computed from those same self-selected labels, so it would look sound while the blind spot grows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because overall accuracy can hide weak areas. But every figure uses labels the model chose, so scams it misses never appear in any of them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recovery is a standard control. But it is a minor IT point beside labels that shape every retrain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model is complex. But scoping the algorithm leaves out the data, where this risk sits.

tips: Eliminate: D scopes the algorithm rather than its data, and C adds a general IT control of minor weight here.
Final two: B beats A because accuracy by scam type is computed from labels the model itself chose, so the scams it misses never show up.
Exam cue: when a model learns only from cases it selected, scope the labeling loop. What it never flags is never learned or measured.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1203 (Engagement Planning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A.2 Scoping an AI Audit Engagement (cover the lifecycle stages in play, including data sourcing, not only the algorithm and its accuracy). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. One model, many regional offices
questions.question: A Nova Scotia home-care agency's model scores how urgently each client needs a nurse; each regional office sets its own visit cutoff. Which addition to the IS auditor's model-focused scope is MOST important?

options.A: Who can view client scores at each regional office
options.B: Change control over each release of the model's code and weights
options.C: A specialist review of the model's training algorithm
options.D: How each local threshold is set, approved and changed

questions.key_concept: A score becomes a decision only at its cutoff; where local staff set cutoffs, scope covers how each is set, approved and changed.
questions.pre_read: Map each part of the system against the planned scope.
questions.correct_explanation: The model only scores; the cutoff turns a score into a nurse visit or none. With each office choosing its own cutoff, the same score can bring a visit in one region and nothing in another, and an unapproved change can quietly cut visits. Scope must cover how those thresholds are set, approved and changed. Release change control over the model would miss this: a cutoff moves with no new model version.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because client scores are sensitive health data. But viewing access is a general privacy control; the cutoffs decide who gets a visit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model releases are the usual change point. But an office can move its cutoff with no release, changing who gets a visit while release control sees nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model is technical. But scoping the algorithm leaves out the decision process where this risk sits.

tips: Eliminate: C scopes the algorithm rather than the decisions, and A adds a general access control over who sees scores.
Final two: D beats B because a cutoff change alters which clients get a visit with no model release, so release change control never sees it.
Exam cue: a model's score is not the decision. Scope the thresholds that turn scores into actions, and who may change them.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1203 (Engagement Planning); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's stand-in model
questions.question: The audit's vetted specialist explains a Kerala cooperative bank's gold-loan model using a simpler surrogate model trained to mimic it, and concludes that declines rest on repayment history. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the conclusion, as the specialist was vetted and is independent
options.B: Compare the surrogate's main factors with the bank's model card
options.C: Check how closely the surrogate's outputs match the real model
options.D: Ask the model's developers to confirm the surrogate's explanation

questions.key_concept: A surrogate model explains itself; its explanations describe the real model only as far as the two agree, so check that agreement first.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the specialist's method can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: A surrogate explains itself, not the bank's model. Its factors describe the real model's declines only as far as the two agree, so the first question is fidelity: how often the surrogate reaches the same decision for the same applicants. The model card is written by the builders and describes intended design; agreeing with it cannot show the surrogate tracks what the deployed model actually does.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the specialist was vetted. But vetting covers competence and objectivity, not whether this method supports this conclusion.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the card documents the intended factors. But it is the builders' description, so matching it cannot show the surrogate mirrors the deployed model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because developers know the model. But builders vouching for a test of their own model is weak, non-independent evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a vetted specialist without evaluating the method, and D asks the builders to vouch for a test of their own model.
Final two: C beats B because a surrogate explains the real model only as far as they agree; a builder-written card cannot show that agreement.
Exam cue: an explanation from a stand-in model covers the stand-in. Check how closely it matches the real model before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. The builder in the audit
questions.question: Only the lead developer understands the code of a Zanzibar tour company's model that assigns guides their tours, and so their pay. How should the IS audit manager BEST use the developer in fairness testing?

options.A: To explain the code, while independent staff design and run tests
options.B: To stay out entirely, with testing deferred until a specialist is hired
options.C: To build the fairness test set, while independent staff run the tests
options.D: To sign off the fairness conclusion as the audit's code expert

questions.key_concept: Builders may explain their model and supply raw data for checking, but the choice of fairness test records and the tests stay independent.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each role would let the developer influence.
questions.correct_explanation: Builders' testing is never independent, and in fairness testing that includes the data: whoever builds the test set chooses the records, group labels and what counts as fair, and those choices can decide the result. The developer can explain the code in walkthroughs, as any auditee can, while independent staff build the test set and run the tests. A raw extract is easy to check against source; a builder's choices are hard to see afterward.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because independence matters. But developers routinely explain systems in walkthroughs; deferring leaves guides' pay untested meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditee-prepared data is common in audits. But building a fairness test set means choosing its records and group labels, which can decide the result.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the developer knows the model best. But a builder signing off their own model's fairness gives no independent assurance.

tips: Eliminate: D has the builder sign off the audit's conclusion, and B treats any contact with the builder as fatal to independence.

Final two: A beats C because building a fairness test set means choosing the records and group labels the result depends on; unlike a raw extract checked against source, that choice must stay independent.
Exam cue: builders may explain their model and supply raw data for checking, but never choose the audit's test cases or design its tests.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Rolling out a drafting tool
questions.question: Before rolling out an approved AI tool that drafts audit test steps, a Tasmanian university's chief audit executive learns auditors at a peer university adopted most drafts unchanged. Which planning step is BEST?

options.A: Rely on the vendor's published accuracy for drafting test steps
options.B: Have auditors rerun each draft to confirm it comes out the same
options.C: Restrict it to low-risk audits and widen use as auditors gain experience
options.D: Train auditors on its typical errors and require each draft reviewed

questions.key_concept: Over-reliance on audit AI is automation bias; plan training on the tool's limits and required review of every output before rollout.
questions.pre_read: Picture the tool in use on an ordinary audit.
questions.correct_explanation: Adopting most drafts unchanged can signal automation bias: fluent, plausible drafts invite acceptance, and the gaps a tool leaves are easy to miss. Training auditors on the errors this tool tends to make, and requiring review of every draft before use, works on the behavior itself. Limiting the tool to low-risk audits reduces what over-reliance can damage, but auditors there can still adopt flawed drafts unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors publish accuracy. But a vendor figure is an input, not validation, and does nothing about over-reliance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consistency feels like checking. But a repeated draft can repeat the same gap; reruns test consistency, not correctness.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because limiting use limits damage. But auditors on low-risk audits can still accept drafts unchecked, and growing familiarity with a fluent tool tends to deepen reliance.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a vendor accuracy figure as a safeguard, and B mistakes a consistent rerun for a check.
Final two: D beats C because restricting where the tool runs limits damage but not the habit; training and required review change how auditors treat drafts.
Exam cue: plan the people side of audit AI. Auditors are trained on the tool's limits and must review every output.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An audit tool on the auditee's model
questions.question: To check 30,000 taxpayer letters drafted by a Basque tax agency's AI tool, its IS audit team plans to use an approved audit tool built on the same vendor model. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The vendor may update the shared model while the checks run
options.B: The audit tool may share the drafting tool's blind spots
options.C: Checking each of the 30,000 letters costs more than a sample
options.D: The agency's managers have not agreed to the tool's criteria

questions.key_concept: A checker built on the same model as the AI it checks tends to share its blind spots, so it is not an independent test.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern by how much it would weaken the audit's conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: A checker built on the same model as the drafter tends to share its mistakes: if the model misreads a rule, the checker likely accepts the misreading. Its errors are correlated with the drafting tool's, so the letters most likely to be wrong are the ones most likely to pass. A model update during the checks is a reproducibility issue to record; it does not undermine validity the way shared blind spots do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hosted models change. Recording the version handles that; shared blind spots would make the checks unreliable even with a fixed version.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because samples are cheaper. But a full-population check is a strength when the tool is valid; cost is not the main risk here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners know their rules. But the auditor selects audit criteria for suitability; management's agreement is never a condition.

tips: Eliminate: C treats full-population testing as the problem, and D gives the auditee a veto over audit criteria.
Final two: B beats A because shared training means shared mistakes; a model update can be recorded, but a checker blind to the same errors passes them.
Exam cue: an AI checking output from the same model is not an independent check. Look for correlated errors before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Label edits in a click-fraud system
questions.question: Testing controls over a Flemish ad network's click-fraud model, retrained weekly on analysts' fraud labels, an IS auditor finds any account manager can edit those labels without a record. What makes this exception MOST significant?

options.A: Edited labels could cut the model's overall accuracy after retraining
options.B: Staff could teach the model to pass their chosen fake clicks
options.C: Edited labels on billed clicks could misstate past advertiser refunds
options.D: Edits to labels about users' clicks would need the users' consent

questions.key_concept: Training labels shape the model: edits nobody records can poison the next retrain, so label changes need access limits and a trail.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each consequence by its likelihood and impact before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Labels are the model's teacher. Because any account manager can change them without a trace, someone could relabel a favored publisher's fake clicks as genuine, and the next weekly retrain would learn to pass clicks like them. That is insider poisoning of training data, and with no record it is hard to detect. Misstated refunds are a real reporting issue, but the poisoned model would keep billing advertisers for fraud week after week.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because bad labels can degrade a model. But edits aimed at chosen clicks barely move overall accuracy; the harm is what the model learns to pass.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because refund figures matter. But the larger harm is forward-looking: each retrain learns from the edited labels and starts passing similar fake clicks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because clicks come from people. But consent is rarely the lawful basis for fraud screening, and the gap here is who can change labels unrecorded.

tips: Eliminate: A expects the edits to show as lower overall accuracy, though targeted relabeling barely moves it, and D turns an integrity gap into a consent question.
Final two: B beats C because edited labels flow into every later retrain, teaching the model to pass fraud; misstated refund history is the smaller harm.
Exam cue: training labels are a control point. Anyone who can change them unrecorded can change the model at its next retrain.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.3.2 (Targeted Poisoning); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
