Batch 8 re-audit: moved from an insurer's claims-fraud model retrained on investigators' labels, which repeated the setting of crisc_d2_174, to an ad network's click-fraud model; option A now turns on the targeted-poisoning fact that overall accuracy barely moves. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reviewing AI invoice summaries
questions.question: Claims handlers at a Saskatchewan pet insurer check each AI summary, written from the AI's text extraction of a scanned veterinary invoice, against that extraction. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion about this control?

options.A: It is reliable if each extraction check is signed and dated
options.B: It is effective, since a person reviews every summary
options.C: It would be stronger if the model rated its own summaries
options.D: It cannot catch errors the extraction and summary share

questions.key_concept: A human check against an AI-made reference cannot catch errors both share; reviewers need the original source, here the scanned invoice.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each check could and could not detect.
questions.correct_explanation: A check is only as independent as its reference. The summary is written from the AI's extraction, so a misread amount or drug name in the extraction reappears in the summary, and comparing the two confirms the error. The design cannot catch shared errors; the scanned invoice is the source to check against. Sign-offs would show checks happened, not that they could find these errors.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because operation needs evidence. But sign-offs prove checks happened; a check against the AI extraction still cannot find errors it shares with the summary.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a person sees every summary. But a human step controls only what the human can detect from the reference given.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because self-rating is cheap. But a model rating its own output repeats its own errors and adds no independent check.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a human step as control by itself, and C has the model check its own output.
Final two: D beats A because sign-offs show the check ran, while a reference built by the same AI cannot reveal errors it shares with the summary.
Exam cue: test what a reviewer compares against. Oversight against AI-made references inherits AI errors; the original source is the true check.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.1 Testing AI Controls and Human Oversight (test design by walking each control through the risk it should address; oversight counts only when reviewers can catch wrong outputs). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Data offered for a fairness test
questions.question: To test whether an Ecuadorian ministry's housing-subsidy model currently treats Kichwa-speaking applicants fairly, the data team offers the IS auditor its labeled training set of 40,000 past applicants. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: It shows the examples learned from, not today's live decisions
options.B: Forty thousand records are too many to analyze completely
options.C: Kichwa speakers may be too few in it for any reliable comparison
options.D: Its 40,000 records were extracted by the data team, not the auditor

questions.key_concept: Training data shows what a model learned from; fairness to a group is tested on a sample of current production decisions.
questions.pre_read: Match the data to where the risk in the question arises.
questions.correct_explanation: Training data shows the examples the model learned from. Fairness to Kichwa-speaking applicants is decided in live scoring, where the current version, its threshold and today's applicants can all differ from the training set. The test belongs on a sample of production decisions, stratified by language. Even a training set with many Kichwa speakers would describe past inputs, not the outcomes applicants now receive.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because volume seems heavy. But analytics handle 40,000 records easily; size is not the issue.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small groups need enough cases. But even plenty of Kichwa rows in training data would not show how live decisions treat them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditee-prepared data needs checking. But even a set the auditor extracted would show past training examples, not live decisions.

tips: Eliminate: B treats data volume as a barrier, and D worries about who extracted data that is the wrong population anyway.
Final two: A beats C because group size matters only once the population is right; the sample must come from live decisions by the current version, stratified by language.
Exam cue: when the risk is in live outcomes, sample production decisions. Training data answers questions about data quality, not current fairness.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF Guideline 2208 (Information Technology Audit Sampling); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.2 Sampling AI Decisions (sample production decisions when the risk is in live outcomes; sample training data only when the objective is data quality). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Population for a ranking model
questions.question: A Slovenian home-repair platform's model ranks local firms whenever a customer posts a job. Which population should the IS auditor BEST sample to test whether it disadvantages women-owned firms?

options.A: Contacted firms, stratified so women-owned firms are enough to compare
options.B: Complaints firms filed about where the rankings placed them
options.C: Every firm ranked for each request, with its position
options.D: Firm records in the data the model was trained on

questions.key_concept: A ranking model's harm lands on those it buries; a population drawn from what users saw or chose excludes them.
questions.pre_read: Name what the model decides before judging any population.
questions.correct_explanation: A ranking model decides who is seen. If it pushes women-owned firms down, customers never view or contact them, so the harm falls on firms absent from any list of contacts. Only every firm ranked for each request, with its position, shows whether women-owned firms sit lower than similar firms. Stratifying contacted firms fixes group size, but every contacted firm was already seen, so the buried firms stay out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because stratifying gives each group enough cases. But every contacted firm was already seen; firms ranked too low to be contacted still cannot enter.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complaints signal problems. But firms buried in rankings rarely know why, so complaints miss this harm.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training data is easy to obtain. But it shows what the model learned from, not where it ranks firms in live use.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on complaints from firms that rarely know they were buried, and D samples training data instead of live rankings.
Final two: C beats A because stratifying fixes group size, but a contacted-firms population structurally excludes the buried firms the test is about.
Exam cue: a ranking model decides who is seen. Build its fairness population from every firm ranked for each request, with its position, not from those users contacted.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF Guideline 2208 (Information Technology Audit Sampling); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.2 Sampling AI Decisions (design an AI sample around where errors hide; for a ranking model the population is everything ranked). Re-angled at the batch 8 re-audit because the first version reused the stem shape and runner-up of aaia_d3_125. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reperforming a generated label
questions.question: A Panamanian telecom's language model labels each customer complaint as reportable to the regulator or not. Which procedure gives the IS auditor the BEST evidence that sampled complaints were labeled correctly?

options.A: Review the accuracy figure the telecom reported to the regulator
options.B: Rerun each sampled complaint through the logged model version and prompt
options.C: Ask the model to explain why it labeled each complaint
options.D: Classify each sampled complaint against the regulator's definition

questions.key_concept: Reperforming an AI judgment means the auditor applies the criteria; rerunning the model checks its consistency, not whether its label was right.
questions.pre_read: Decide what the procedure must prove before choosing one.
questions.correct_explanation: Correct labeling is a judgment against the regulator's definition, so the auditor reperforms that judgment on the sampled complaints. Rerunning the logged version and prompt shows whether the model repeats its own label, and with generated output it may not even do that. Either way, a model repeating an answer says nothing about whether the answer was right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is formal reporting. But it is the auditee's own figure, not evidence the auditor obtained on these complaints.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rerunning the deciding version is classic AI reperformance. But it tests whether the label repeats, not whether it meets the definition.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because explanations seem revealing. But a model's account of its own label is more generated text, not evidence it was right.

tips: Eliminate: C asks the model to vouch for itself, and A relies on the auditee's own reported figure.
Final two: D beats B because a rerun shows whether the model repeats its label; only applying the definition shows whether the label was right.
Exam cue: to test whether an AI judgment was correct, make the judgment yourself against the criteria. Reruns test reproducibility, not correctness.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.3 Reperformance and Full-Population Testing (prefer evidence the auditor produces: reperform the judgment against the criteria). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reasons sent to declined applicants
questions.question: A Chilean dental chain's payment-plan model declines patients; each decline letter lists reasons its explanation tool produced. Which procedure BEST shows the IS auditor that each sampled letter carries the tool's reasons for that decline?

options.A: Check each letter's reasons against the approved reason list
options.B: Recompute reasons with the deciding version and the logged inputs
options.C: Ask the model owner how the explanation tool picks its reasons
options.D: Confirm each letter was sent within the required number of days

questions.key_concept: A decline letter's reasons should match what the explanation tool gives for that decision; recompute them with the deciding version and logged inputs.
questions.pre_read: Read each option for what it would actually prove.
questions.correct_explanation: An approved reason can still be wrong for that patient. Each letter's reasons come from the explanation tool applied to one model version and one patient's inputs, so the auditor reruns the tool on the archived version with each sampled patient's logged inputs and compares the result with the letter. That shows the letter carries this decision's explanation; whether the explanation method is faithful is a separate validation question.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approved wording is a compliance control. But an allowed reason can be wrong for that patient; recomputing shows whether the letter carries the tool's reasons for that decline.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the owner knows the tool. But a description of the method is not evidence about any sampled letter.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because timeliness is often required. But it tests when letters went out, not whether they carry the tool's reasons for each decline.

tips: Eliminate: C accepts the owner's description, and D tests timing rather than the reasons.
Final two: B beats A because the approved list shows a reason is allowed; recomputing with the deciding version and logged inputs shows whether the letter carries that decision's reasons.
Exam cue: an AI explanation is a computed output tied to one version and one input. Recompute it from those to test the letter; validate the method separately.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.3 Reperformance and Full-Population Testing (a logged decision can be reproduced only if the same model version and inputs are still available). Release audit, 18 Nov 2026: stem now asks whether each letter carries that decline's computed reasons, separating the item from aaia_d3_127. Release audit fix round 2, 18 Nov 2026: stem asks whether each letter carries the tool's reasons, not whether the reasons are right, to agree with aaia_d3_127. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An agent's tool list
questions.question: A Corsican campsite group's AI booking agent has a tool list in its configuration that excludes refunds. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether the agent can issue refunds?

options.A: The vendor's statement that its agents follow their tool lists
options.B: Tool-call logs showing no refund attempts by the agent
options.C: The payment system's permissions granted to the agent's credentials
options.D: The agent's own answer when asked whether it can refund

questions.key_concept: An agent's real powers are the access its credentials hold in connected systems, not the tools its configuration lists.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how directly they answer the question asked.
questions.correct_explanation: What an agent can do is set by the access its credentials hold, not by the tool list it is given. If the payment system lets the agent's account issue refunds, a manipulated prompt, a new tool or a configuration change could use that access. Logs showing no refund attempts describe past behavior; they cannot show the agent is unable to refund tomorrow.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the agent. But a vendor's general statement is not evidence about this agent's access.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because logs are system evidence. But no attempts so far shows behavior, not capability; the access would still be there to misuse.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is direct. But an agent's account of itself is generated text, and it may not know its real access.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a vendor's general claim, and D takes the agent's word about itself.
Final two: C beats B because logs show what the agent has done, while the payment system's permissions show what it can do.
Exam cue: to know an AI agent's limits, inspect the access its credentials hold in each connected system, not its instructions or history.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.1 Sources of AI Evidence (match the evidence to the question; records systems produce outrank documents and statements). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Which version answered
questions.question: A Maldivian dive-tour operator's vendor-hosted assistant gave different cancellation terms in April and May; the operator's change log shows no change. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor which model version gave each answer?

options.A: The model identifier recorded with each response
options.B: The operator's contract naming the model the vendor supplies
options.C: The assistant's reply when asked which version it runs
options.D: The vendor's published release notes for the period

questions.key_concept: Per-answer evidence of a hosted model's version comes from what the service records with each response, not from the vendor's general notes.
questions.pre_read: Match the evidence to the exact question asked.
questions.correct_explanation: The question is which version produced each answer, so the evidence must be recorded per answer: the model identifier the service returns with every response, kept in the operator's logs. The change log shows nothing because a vendor can update a hosted model without the operator acting. Release notes describe changes in general and cannot tie a version to one customer's answer; the identifier is only as precise as the vendor's versioning.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the contract is formal. But it states what should be supplied, not what actually answered each customer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is direct. But a model's statement about itself is generated text, often wrong about its own version.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors announce changes. But notes describe changes in general and cannot show which version answered a given customer.

tips: Eliminate: C takes the model's word about itself, and B shows what was promised, not what ran.
Final two: A beats D because release notes describe changes in general, while the identifier recorded with each response ties a version to each answer.
Exam cue: for hosted AI, ask which record ties an output to a version, input and time. Per-transaction logs beat vendor announcements.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.1 Sources of AI Evidence (decision and prompt logs, with model version and configuration history, show what happened in production). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A year without drift alerts
questions.question: A Vietnamese seafood processor's drift monitor for its freshness-grading model ran every day this year, per the scheduler, and raised no alerts. Which further evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether monitoring operated effectively?

options.A: The monitor's configuration export taken at fieldwork
options.B: The model owner's written statement that the model has not drifted
options.C: The list of staff who would receive the monitor's alerts
options.D: The alert limits in force over the period, with each change

questions.key_concept: A drift monitor that never alerts proves little unless its limits could catch drift all period; limits too wide, or widened, silence a running monitor.
questions.pre_read: Consider every reason a monitor might show no alerts.
questions.correct_explanation: A monitor that ran daily and never alerted shows either no drift or limits that could not catch it. Limits set too wide at the start, or widened after nuisance alerts, silence a monitor without stopping it. The limits in force over the period, with each change, show whether it could have alerted and whether anyone loosened it. A configuration export at fieldwork shows only today's settings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it shows the current limits. But one export shows today's settings, not whether limits were widened or reset during the year.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because owners know their models. But inquiry alone is weak evidence and cannot show the monitor worked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because alerts must reach someone. But no alert fired, so who would receive one cannot explain the silence; the limits can.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on inquiry alone, and C checks who receives alerts when none fired.
Final two: D beats A because a fieldwork export shows today's limits; the limits in force over the period, with each change, show whether the monitor could alert all year.
Exam cue: silence from an AI monitor is evidence only if its limits could catch drift. Check the limits in force across the period, not just its runs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-6 (Configuration Settings)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.2 Sufficiency, Reliability and Preservation of AI Evidence (prefer records over time, such as alert histories, to screenshots or dashboards showing one moment). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Archiving a retired allocation model
questions.question: A Danish student-housing foundation will retire its room-allocation model and archive only its trained weights, so appeals can rerun disputed applicant rankings. Which additional item is MOST important for the IS auditor to have preserved?

options.A: The approval memo setting the model's retirement date
options.B: The code that turned raw records into the model's inputs
options.C: A cryptographic hash proving the archived weights are unaltered
options.D: The data science team's slide deck that explains the model

questions.key_concept: Neither weights nor code alone can rerun a decision; keep the weights with the input-preparation code, settings and the logged raw inputs.
questions.pre_read: Note what the archive already holds before judging what is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: Weights alone cannot reproduce a ranking. Each decision came from raw application records turned into model inputs by preparation code, then scored by the weights; without that code, nobody can feed a past application back through the model to check a disputed ranking. A hash proves the weights were not altered, which matters, but it protects a file that cannot rerun any decision on its own.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retirement needs approval. But the memo records a decision, not anything needed to rerun past rankings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because integrity matters for evidence. But a hash protects weights that cannot rerun a ranking without the code that prepared their inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it explains the model. But builders' slides describe design; they cannot reproduce any applicant's ranking.

tips: Eliminate: D keeps a builder's description, and A keeps a governance record that cannot rerun a ranking.
Final two: B beats C because a hash proves integrity of weights that, without the input preparation code, cannot reproduce any decision.
Exam cue: preserve what reruns a decision: the version, its input preparation, settings and inputs, not just the trained file.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.2 Sufficiency, Reliability and Preservation of AI Evidence (ask owners to preserve versions, configurations and logs before planned changes overwrite them). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A policy rule the tool reported
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI tool, given only a Guatemalan coffee cooperative's IT policies, states that passwords must be at least 12 characters. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Locate the rule in the policy text before relying on it
options.B: Rerun the question to see whether the answer repeats
options.C: Confirm every policy file was supplied to the tool
options.D: Accept it, since these policies were its sole input

questions.key_concept: A generative tool can fill gaps in documents with plausible general knowledge; confirm each statement in the source before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask where a plausible statement like this could have come from.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool can blend the documents it was given with what it learned in training, so a common rule such as a 12-character minimum may appear even if the cooperative's policies never say it. The auditor finds the requirement in the policy text before relying on it. Confirming that every policy file was supplied checks the input, but even with every file supplied the tool can add the rule from training.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consistency feels reassuring. But a tool can repeat the same unsupported statement every time.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because missing input often causes wrong answers. But even with every file supplied, the tool can add the rule from training; only the policy text verifies it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool was given nothing else. But generative tools can add plausible rules from training, so the statement may appear in no policy.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a repeated answer as verified, and D accepts the statement because of what the tool was given.
Final two: A beats C because even with every policy file supplied, a generative tool can add a common rule from training; only the policy text shows it exists.
Exam cue: AI statements about documents can come from training rather than the documents. Confirm each one in the source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.3 Evidence Produced by AI Tools (treat AI output as a lead until it is corroborated against source records). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Two prompts, two answers
questions.question: Asked whether 80 firewall rule changes at a Sardinian airport were approved, an IS auditor's approved AI tool said all were; asked which lacked approval, it named six. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Ask the tool which of its two answers is right
options.B: Treat the six as unapproved, since that prompt was more skeptical
options.C: Check every change against the approval records directly
options.D: Have the tool cite the approval record for each change

questions.key_concept: Generated answers lean toward a question's framing, so two prompts can yield opposite results; neither is evidence until checked against records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the difference between the two answers reveals about both.
questions.correct_explanation: Generated answers tend to follow the framing of the question: asked to confirm, a model leans toward confirming; asked to find faults, it leans toward finding some. Neither answer is evidence. With only 80 changes, the auditor checks each against the approval records. Having the tool cite a record for each change only adds generated text that framing can steer; a cited record proves nothing until opened.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tool produced both answers. But its verdict on itself is more generated text, not evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a fault-finding question looks like professional skepticism. But framing steers generated answers: some of the six may be invented, and the other 74 stay untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a cited record looks traceable. But a generated citation is more generated text: it can follow the framing or name a record that says otherwise.

tips: Eliminate: A asks the tool to judge itself, and B mistakes a fault-finding prompt for professional skepticism.
Final two: C beats D because a citation the tool writes is more generated text, which framing can steer; only the approval records themselves are evidence.
Exam cue: when rewording a prompt changes the answer, neither answer is evidence. Go to the source records.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C.3 Evidence Produced by AI Tools (neither asking the tool to check itself nor rerunning it proves accuracy; only the sources do). Final round, 13 Nov 2026: B and D now carry the stem terms "approved" and "change", so the key no longer echoes them alone. Re-audit, 13 Nov 2026: D (rerun) replaced with a tool-citation option a careful CISA auditor might choose, so the framing and confabulation fact decides the final two; B is now eliminated. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A conversation export
questions.question: Testing a Malaysian cooking-gas distributor's chatbot for unsafe advice, an IS auditor gets a log export matching the platform's chat count but keeping only each chat's first 20 turns. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: None, since the chat count matches the platform's own total
options.B: Later turns, where long chats tend to go wrong, are missing
options.C: Twenty turns per chat leaves too much text for a manual test
options.D: Matching counts do not show each kept turn was copied accurately

questions.key_concept: An export can match record counts yet drop content; with chatbots, harmful answers often come late in long conversations.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the test's objective.
questions.correct_explanation: Unsafe advice in a support chat often comes late: long conversations drift, and users who push repeatedly can wear down a chatbot's safeguards over many turns. An export cut at 20 turns removes exactly that part of the population while the chat count still matches. Accurate copying of the kept turns matters, but it cannot restore turns the export never held.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because counts reconcile. But a matching count shows every chat is present, not that each chat is whole.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because volume seems heavy. But analytics and sampling handle volume; the issue is what the export leaves out.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because field accuracy matters. But copying errors would affect turns the export kept; the bigger gap is the turns it dropped.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a count reconciliation as proof of completeness, and C treats volume as the problem.
Final two: B beats D because accurate copying cannot restore dropped turns, and long chats are where safeguards wear down.
Exam cue: reconcile content as well as counts. For chatbots, a truncated conversation can hide exactly the answers you are testing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.1 Completeness and Accuracy of Audit Data (populations can be shaped upstream by filters, retention settings or logging choices; reconcile content as well as counts). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Data tidied by a generative tool
questions.question: An IS auditor had an approved generative AI tool standardize date and name formats in a Bhutanese hydropower company's 18,000-row payroll extract before testing all rows for duplicate payees. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Check a random sample of 25 cleaned rows against the original extract
options.B: Ask the tool to list every value it changed
options.C: Rerun the tool and compare the two cleaned files
options.D: Script a comparison of every value with the original extract

questions.key_concept: Generative tools asked to tidy data can silently alter values; compare the output with the original field by field before analyzing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool may have done besides formatting.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool asked to tidy formats can also change content: a name reworded to match another, a digit dropped, a value it judged wrong replaced, with no error raised. A duplicate-payee test depends on every name and value, so a scripted comparison of every value with the original extract, allowing for the intended format changes, finds each silent edit. A sample of 25 estimates how often values changed but leaves the altered rows unidentified.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sampling is standard. But a sample estimates a rate; it cannot identify which of 18,000 rows were altered before the duplicate test runs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is quick. But the tool's account of its changes is generated text and can miss what it altered.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because matching runs feel like a check. But two runs compare the tool with itself; only the original extract shows which values changed.

tips: Eliminate: C compares the tool with itself, and B asks the tool to report on itself.
Final two: D beats A because a sample only estimates how often values changed, while a scripted full comparison finds every altered value before analysis.
Exam cue: when a generative tool transforms audit data, compare its output with the source in full. Reruns and self-reports miss silent edits.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.1 Completeness and Accuracy of Audit Data (an extract is a copy; compare copy and source before testing, and do not trust a count alone). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A fake-supplier tool's test result
questions.question: A Dutch flower auction's audit team measured 90% precision for its AI fake-supplier tool on 1,000 test supplier records, half of them fake; under 1% of live records are fake. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: A test on 1,000 records says nothing about larger volumes
options.B: The vendor's own accuracy figure should replace this test
options.C: A far larger share of its flags will be false in use
options.D: It may miss kinds of fake suppliers absent from the test set

questions.key_concept: Precision depends on how common the target is; a test set rich in exceptions overstates precision when exceptions are rare in live data.
questions.pre_read: Compare the test conditions with the live data the tool will meet.
questions.correct_explanation: Precision depends on how common the target is. In a test set half full of fake suppliers, false alarms were few beside the many true hits. Live, where fakes are under 1%, the same false-alarm rate applies to almost every record, so most flags may be false and follow-up effort balloons. Missing unseen kinds of fakes is a real risk, but nothing in these facts points to it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because volume grows. But error rates do not depend on volume; the share of fake suppliers is what changed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors publish figures. But a vendor figure is an input, not validation on the auditor's data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because test sets can miss patterns. But the stated fact is the gap between test and live fake rates, which inflates false alarms.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses volume with prevalence, and B swaps validation for a vendor figure.
Final two: C beats D because the facts given are the test and live fake rates; at under 1%, the same tool's flags will be mostly false.
Exam cue: check that an audit tool was validated at a realistic exception rate. Precision measured on balanced data overstates live precision.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.2 AI-Assisted Audit Analytics and Tool Validation (validate the tool on known outcomes and measure both errors before reliance). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Validating a generative checker
questions.question: Before relying on a generative AI checker for every shipment, a Moroccan argan-oil exporter's auditors ran it once on 150 documents, each with one independently planted error; it caught 141. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: A repeat on the same documents could catch different errors
options.B: A 150-document test is too small to measure a reliable rate
options.C: The vendor's benchmark would be a better validation source
options.D: Documents with planted errors cannot validate an audit tool

questions.key_concept: Generative tools can vary run to run; validating one on a single run measures one draw, not how reliably it catches errors.
questions.pre_read: Judge the test as a reviewer of the work paper would.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative tools can give different results on the same input from run to run, so one run's 141 catches is a single draw, not a measured rate. Validation should repeat the runs and record how much the catches vary before the team relies on the tool. More documents would narrow the estimate for one run but would not show how much results shift between runs.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because small tests give loose estimates. But a larger single run still hides how much results vary between runs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because benchmarks are published. But a vendor benchmark is an input, not validation on this audit's data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because planted data feels unreal. But planted test cases are a sound method when made independently of the tool, as these were.

tips: Eliminate: D rules out planted test cases, a sound method when built independently, and C swaps validation for a vendor benchmark.
Final two: A beats B because a bigger single run still measures one draw; generated output varies, so validation must show how much results shift between runs.
Exam cue: validate a generative audit tool across repeated runs. One run's result is a sample of its behavior, not its rate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.13 (Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.2 AI-Assisted Audit Analytics and Tool Validation (validate the tool before relying on it; generative tools can vary between runs, so validate over repeated runs). Final round, 13 Nov 2026: numbers and the sample-size distractor reworded so the stem no longer mirrors aaia_d3_073. Re-audit, 13 Nov 2026: stem now says the tool will be relied on for every shipment, so repeated use, not sample size, decides it. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Whistleblower notes in an approved service
questions.question: A Sicilian ceramics maker's IS auditor plans to summarize whistleblower notes in an approved AI service whose contract bars training on inputs but keeps them 30 days for abuse review. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The summary would need disclosing as AI use in the report
options.B: The summary may distort the whistleblower's key allegations
options.C: None, since the contract bars training on the notes
options.D: Provider staff may see who the whistleblower is

questions.key_concept: A bar on training does not bar retention; check an AI service's retention and human-review terms before confidential audit data goes in.
questions.pre_read: Read each contract term for what it does and does not limit.
questions.correct_explanation: A bar on training stops the provider learning from the notes, not keeping them. Here inputs stay 30 days and may be read by provider staff checking for abuse, and allegations are the kind of content such review can flag, so the whistleblower's identity could reach people outside the audit. A distorted summary is a real risk, but the auditor can check it against the notes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because methodology may require disclosure. But disclosure is a reporting step, not the risk of the provider keeping confidential notes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because summaries can be wrong. But the auditor can check a summary against the notes; exposed details cannot be taken back.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a training bar is the protection most often sought. But it does not stop retention or human review of inputs, which this contract allows.

tips: Eliminate: A mistakes a disclosure duty for the main risk, and B names a risk the auditor can check against the notes.
Final two: D beats C because barring training does not bar keeping: inputs held for abuse review can be read by provider staff.
Exam cue: read AI service terms for retention and human review, not just training use, before audit data goes in.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.3 Reproducibility and Confidentiality in AI-Assisted Audits (contract terms and data classification decide which audit data an AI service may receive). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Rerunning a long chat
questions.question: Rerunning an IS auditor's 15-turn AI chat on a Turkmen gas utility's contracts from the recorded version, settings, final prompt and input, a reviewer gets very different results. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The reviewer lacked the auditor's access rights to the tool
options.B: Earlier messages that shaped the output were not kept
options.C: Hosted models vary slightly between runs, even with fixed settings
options.D: The auditor's output file was not attached to the work paper

questions.key_concept: A chat's output depends on every earlier turn; record the whole conversation, not only the final prompt, so AI-assisted work can be rerun.
questions.pre_read: Match the size of the difference to its likely cause.
questions.correct_explanation: A chat's answer depends on everything earlier in the conversation, not just the last prompt. Fourteen earlier turns of instructions and corrections shaped the auditor's result, so replaying only the final prompt asks the model a different question. Hosted models do vary between runs, but that explains small differences, not very different results.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because access can block work. But access rights decide whether the reviewer can run the tool, not what it answers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hosted models are not perfectly reproducible. But that explains small differences; very different results point to missing context.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the output is evidence. But keeping the output does not let anyone rerun the work or explain a difference.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses keeping output with reproducing work, and A blames access, which cannot change answers.
Final two: B beats C because run-to-run variation explains small differences, while missing earlier turns change the question itself.
Exam cue: for chat-based AI work, the conversation is the input. Record every turn with the version and settings.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3D.3 Reproducibility and Confidentiality in AI-Assisted Audits (a rerun can match only when the tool version, settings, prompts and input data all match the original). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Stating a test result
questions.question: An IS auditor put 200 test questions to a Hungarian vehicle-registration office's assistant in May and found 12 wrong answers; the vendor updates the model monthly. Which condition statement is BEST for the finding?

options.A: Twelve of 200 test answers from May's version were wrong
options.B: Applicants may have missed registration deadlines after wrong answers
options.C: The assistant answers 12 in 200 registration questions wrongly
options.D: May's test accuracy is below an acceptable standard

questions.key_concept: A condition states what was found and on what basis; for a hosted model, tie the result to the version and test that produced it.
questions.pre_read: Check that each statement claims no more than the test showed.
questions.correct_explanation: A condition states what the auditor found, on what basis. Twelve wrong answers came from 200 test questions put to the version live in May; the vendor has updated the model since, and test questions are not a random draw of applicants' questions. Stating a general 6% error rate claims more than the test showed, and management could rightly challenge it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because harm matters. But this is the finding's effect, and stated as possible harm it does not describe what was found.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses the test's own figures. But it states them as a general rate for all questions and for versions since May.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it judges performance. But it names no criteria and no result, so it is a conclusion, not a condition.

tips: Eliminate: D gives a judgment with no facts or criteria, and B states the effect rather than the condition.
Final two: A beats C because a monthly-updated model and a set of test questions support a statement about that test and version, not a general rate.
Exam cue: state AI test results with their basis: version, period and sample. Hosted models change, so unqualified rates overclaim.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.1 Writing AI Audit Findings (condition: what the auditor found against the criteria, on a stated basis). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Five degraded models
questions.question: An IS auditor finds five of a Jordanian potash producer's models degraded after retraining; its release reviews cover only code, and no code was altered. How should the auditor BEST report these?

options.A: As five findings recommending each model be retrained again
options.B: As five findings, each one rated by the harm its model caused
options.C: As one finding on the change process, citing all five models
options.D: As one finding on model monitoring, naming the five models

questions.key_concept: When several AI failures share one control gap, report the gap as the cause, with each failure as its effect.
questions.pre_read: Read the facts for cause, then for effect.
questions.correct_explanation: Five models degraded after retraining, and none was validated because release reviews cover only code while a retrain alters no code. That gap is the shared cause, so one finding on the change process, citing the five models as effects, targets the control. A finding on monitoring treats detection after release; the unvalidated models reached production through the change gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining fixes errors. But another retrain through the same gap repeats the change that caused the problem.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because each model's harm differs. But separate findings hide the shared cause, so management fixes symptoms and the next retrain repeats them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring catches degradation. But it detects harm after release; the retrains reached production unvalidated because the change process skipped them.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats the uncontrolled retrain as the fix, and B splits one shared cause into five symptoms.
Final two: C beats D because monitoring only spots degradation after release, while the change process let unvalidated retrains into production.
Exam cue: a retrain is a change even when no code changes. When several models fail after retraining, report the change gap as the cause.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.1 Writing AI Audit Findings (cause: why it happened, named as the control gap). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. An action plan for a replaced model
questions.question: Management's action plan for a Honduran crop insurer's finding of no pre-release fairness testing is one fairness test, before go-live, of its new, monthly-updated vendor claims model. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The test would use past claims rather than the model's live decisions
options.B: Validators may not see the vendor's training data for the fairness test
options.C: The vendor model may be less accurate for local crop types
options.D: Each later version would reach claimants without a fairness test

questions.key_concept: Each vendor model update is a release, so an action plan for a missing pre-release test must cover every version, not just the first.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the plan commits to with what the finding said was missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding's cause was releases reaching claimants without a fairness test. Each monthly vendor update is a new release, because it can change how claims are decided, yet the plan tests only the first version. From the second month, claimants would again face untested versions, so the plan leaves the cause in place. Testing past claims before go-live is normal; live outcomes are checked after release, at follow-up.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because production evidence is strong. But a pre-release test has to use past claims; live decisions are tested after go-live, at follow-up.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data can reveal sources of bias. But a fairness test compares outcomes for groups of claims; it does not need the vendor's training data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because local fit matters. But nothing points to an accuracy problem; the finding was about untested releases, which the plan leaves recurring.

tips: Eliminate: C raises an accuracy risk the facts never point to, and B assumes a fairness test needs the vendor's training data, when it compares outcomes.
Final two: D beats A because each monthly vendor update is a release; one test before go-live leaves every later version untested. Past claims are normal for a pre-release test.
Exam cue: when an action plan fixes a missing pre-release control, check it covers every release. A vendor model that updates is released again each time.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3E.2 Rating, Reporting and Follow-Up of AI Findings (record management's response with owners, actions and dates; the action must reach the cause, and each vendor update is a release). Review round 1, 13 Nov 2026: re-angled from a follow-up closure after model replacement (the frame of aaia_d3_048) to evaluating management's action plan. Review round 2, 13 Nov 2026: option D reworded so no stem word is echoed only in the key. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. A vendor's fix in management's response
questions.question: Responding to a finding that its vendor-hosted prescription-check model blocks valid orders, a Lithuanian online pharmacy commits to a vendor retrain next quarter to block fewer orders. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Record the vendor's date and retest blocked orders at follow-up
options.B: Ask which internal manager sets limits for both error types
options.C: Accept the response, as the hosted model belongs to the vendor
options.D: Lower the finding's rating, since a retrain is now scheduled

questions.key_concept: Retraining a model to cut one error can raise the other, so the organization's owner sets limits for both before a vendor's fix.
questions.pre_read: Read the response for what it commits to and what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: Retraining a model to block fewer orders can shift its errors: fewer valid orders are blocked, but more invalid prescriptions may pass. Only the pharmacy can decide how much of each error is acceptable, so the action needs an internal owner who sets limits for both before the vendor retrains. Retesting blocked orders at follow-up checks only one error, with no limit to judge the retrained model against.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retesting is sound follow-up. But it checks only blocked orders; a model retrained to block fewer may pass invalid prescriptions, and the response limits neither error.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor controls the model. But the pharmacy answers for orders decided with it; accountability cannot pass to the vendor.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because action is planned. But ratings follow the likelihood and impact of harm, and valid orders stay blocked until a retrain works.

tips: Eliminate: C hands accountability to the vendor, and D lowers a rating because a retrain is promised.
Final two: B beats A because a retrain to block fewer orders may pass more invalid prescriptions, so an internal owner sets limits for both errors first; a retest of blocked orders checks one.
Exam cue: a model retrained to cut one error often raises the other. Before accepting the action, ask who in the organization sets limits for both.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Ratings an AI tool suggested
questions.question: A Monaco casino group's draft IS audit report rates each finding as the audit's approved, validated AI tool suggested, with no auditor's reasoning recorded for any rating. What is the chief audit executive's BEST action?

options.A: Keep the ratings, since the tool was validated on past audit findings
options.B: Have auditors disclose in the report that AI suggested the ratings
options.C: Have auditors set each rating from likelihood and impact
options.D: Ask the tool's vendor to confirm the ratings are accurate

questions.key_concept: A finding's rating is an audit judgment; an AI tool may suggest one, but auditors set and own each rating from the evidence.
questions.pre_read: Read the draft as the audit committee will rely on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A rating tells leaders how urgently to act, and it is the auditors' judgment, made from each finding's likelihood and impact. Ratings adopted with no recorded reasoning suggest the auditors deferred to the tool. Validation on past findings shows the tool's suggestions tend to fit; it does not judge each finding's evidence, so keeping the ratings leaves no auditor judgment on record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a validated audit tool's output is usually relied on. But a rating is a judgment; validation makes the suggestion useful input, not the auditors' conclusion.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because material AI use should be disclosed. But disclosure describes the method; it does not make ratings nobody judged the audit's own.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors know their tools. But accountability for audit ratings stays with the audit function, never the vendor.

tips: Eliminate: B describes how the ratings were made without judging any of them, and D shifts accountability to the vendor.
Final two: C beats A because validation makes the tool's suggestions useful input, not judgments; auditors must rate each finding from its own likelihood and impact.
Exam cue: AI may suggest, auditors conclude. Ratings, like findings, are judgments the audit owns.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.4 (Accountable and Transparent)

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. A specialist's AI-assisted analysis
questions.question: An external specialist's report supporting a Bosnian telecom audit says its network-traffic analysis was AI-assisted, giving no detail. Before relying on it in the audit report, what should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Find out what the AI did and what the specialist then checked
options.B: Rerun the analysis with the audit team's own approved AI tool
options.C: Reperform a sample of the specialist's reported findings
options.D: Rely on it, since the specialist is responsible for their methods

questions.key_concept: Using another's AI-assisted work, the auditor must learn how the AI was used and what was verified before relying on it as audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the auditor would need to defend this analysis later.
questions.correct_explanation: Using another's work means understanding how it was produced, and part of this work was produced by AI in ways nobody has described. The auditor needs to know what the tool did and which outputs the specialist verified against data before the analysis can support a conclusion the auditor will own. Reperforming a sample of the reported findings checks what the specialist found, not what the AI may have screened out before anyone looked.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems independent. But a different tool's rerun is another unvalidated output, not an understanding of this one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it checks only what was reported; it cannot show what the AI screened out before the specialist looked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because specialists own their methods. But the auditor remains responsible for conclusions built on their work.

tips: Eliminate: D shifts accountability to the specialist, and B adds a second unexamined AI output.
Final two: A beats C because reperforming reported findings cannot show what the AI left out; the auditor first learns what it did and what was checked.
Exam cue: AI inside someone else's work is still evidence you own. Learn how it was produced and verified before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Rating a test-selection model
questions.question: An IS audit manager is rating the likelihood of harm from a Japanese anti-doping agency's model that picks athletes for surprise tests. Which fact should MOST raise the likelihood rating?

options.A: It has gone four years without an internal audit
options.B: It runs a deep neural network instead of fixed scoring rules
options.C: Its athletes' data may be stored with a cloud host abroad
options.D: People it screens can learn what it misses and adapt

questions.key_concept: Where screened people can probe and adapt to a model, its misses tend to grow, raising the likelihood of harm in a risk ranking.
questions.pre_read: Read what is being rated, then test each option against that measure.
questions.correct_explanation: Athletes who dope gain by studying which profiles go unpicked and changing what they do, so unless the model keeps pace, it misses more over time; that evasion raises the likelihood of harm. Four years without an audit matters when scheduling the audit plan, but it says nothing about how likely the model itself is to fail, which is what this rating measures.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit gaps feed audit planning. But time since the last audit says nothing about how likely the model itself is to fail.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complex models feel riskier. But complexity is not likelihood of harm; a simple model facing adaptive people can fail more often.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data leaving Japan is a real concern. But hosting location bears on privacy and legal impact, not on how likely selection errors are.

tips: Eliminate: B treats technical complexity as risk, and C is a hosting and privacy matter, not how likely selection errors are.
Final two: D beats A because people who adapt to a model make its misses grow; audit recency guides scheduling, not the model's chance of failing.
Exam cue: When the people a model screens gain by avoiding it, expect evasion and rate likelihood higher.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.2 (Evasion Attacks and Mitigations); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Risk Assessment in Planning)

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Scoping a tuned image generator
questions.question: An IS auditor's draft scope for a Finnish furniture brand's catalog-image generator, tuned on its archive and on agency photos licensed for catalog use, covers output review, access and hosting. Which addition is MOST important?

options.A: The approval step for each image before catalog use
options.B: The license terms on training for each photo set
options.C: The vendor's published safety scores for its base model
options.D: Output checks for resemblance to the licensed agency photos

questions.key_concept: An AI audit scope covers data sourcing, including the right to train on each data set, not only how outputs are reviewed.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the draft already covers with what each option would add.
questions.correct_explanation: The agency photos are licensed for catalog use, but tuning a generator on them is a different use, which the license may not cover. Scoping the terms for each photo set covers the data-sourcing stage, where the right to use data is settled. Resemblance checks on outputs can catch near-copies, but a model can learn from licensed photos without copying any one of them, so those checks cannot show the training was permitted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because published images need sign-off. But the draft scope already covers output review; the gap is upstream, in the training data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because base-model safety matters. But the brand's own tuning data and its rights are what this scope is missing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because near-copies are a real output risk. But checking outputs cannot show whether the photos were licensed for training at all.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats output review the scope already covers, and C looks at the vendor's base model rather than the brand's own tuning data.
Final two: B beats D because output checks catch near-copies, while only the license terms show whether training on the photos was allowed.
Exam cue: Training is its own use of data. Scope the rights to train, not only the outputs.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Co-sourcing an AI specialist
questions.question: IS audit's co-sourced specialist, who has validated banks' credit-scoring models for years, will assess a Philippine rural bank's AI agent that chats with members and moves funds between their accounts. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Their skills may not cover prompt injection or agent permissions
options.B: IS audit cannot keep responsibility for co-sourced work
options.C: The specialist may have worked for the agent's developer
options.D: Members' chats would be shared outside the bank

questions.key_concept: A specialist must be competent for the AI risks in scope; credit-model validation does not cover prompt injection or agent permissions.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the question actually states.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that chats with members and moves money is exposed to prompt injection and depends on its tool permissions, risks that years of credit-model validation may never have covered. IS audit must check that the specialist's competence fits these risks before relying on the work. Past ties to the agent's developer would matter, but nothing given suggests any, while the skills gap follows directly from the facts.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because outsiders do the testing. But co-sourcing keeps responsibility with IS audit, which directs and reviews the specialist's work.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because objectivity must always be checked. But nothing suggests ties to the developer here, while the stated skills point to a clear competence gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because chats hold personal data. But specialists work under audit's confidentiality terms; sharing evidence with them is normal.

tips: Eliminate: D treats normal evidence sharing with a bound specialist as the risk, and B misreads co-sourcing, which leaves responsibility with IS audit.
Final two: A beats C because the stated skills do not fit an agent's main risks, while ties to the developer are only a guess here.
Exam cue: Match the specialist to the kind of AI. Statistical modeling skills do not cover agents and language models.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1206 (Using the Work of Other Experts); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1006 (Proficiency); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents)

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Deciding audit uses of AI
questions.question: A Lithuanian state energy group's AI governance committee set data rules for its approved generative tool and offers to approve which audit tasks may use it. What is the chief audit executive's BEST response?

options.A: Accept both, since the committee approves high-impact AI uses
options.B: Let it approve audit tasks; apply audit's own data rules
options.C: Follow its data rules; approve audit tasks in the audit methodology
options.D: Approve audit tasks; replace its data rules with audit's own

questions.key_concept: Auditors follow enterprise AI data rules as users, but the chief audit executive approves audit uses of AI in the methodology.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each choice would mean for the next audit that uses the tool.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee's data rules protect the organization's data in that tool, and auditors, as users, follow them. Which audit tasks may use AI is a decision about audit method, so the chief audit executive makes it in the methodology, under the audit committee's oversight, to keep independence. Replacing the enterprise data rules with audit's own confuses independence with exemption from data controls.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the committee approves high-impact AI uses. But it is management, and choosing audit tasks would let management shape how audit gathers evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems to share the decisions. But it reverses them: management would shape how audit gathers evidence, and auditors would set aside rules protecting the organization's data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because independence matters. But independence covers how audit works; it does not exempt auditors from rules protecting the organization's data.

tips: Eliminate: A lets management choose audit tasks, and B reverses the split, handing audit's methods to management and setting aside the enterprise data rules.
Final two: C beats D because independence covers how audit works, not exemption from the data rules that protect the organization's information.
Exam cue: Auditors follow enterprise AI data rules as users; the chief audit executive decides which audit tasks may use AI.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1002 (Organizational Independence); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented)

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing a model-based order screen
questions.question: An IS auditor plans to test a Czech porcelain maker's language-model order screen for banned glaze chemicals with one order, relying on tested change controls over its pinned version. What is the plan's GREATEST weakness?

options.A: One test cannot show the screen ran through the year
options.B: The pinned version may lag behind the vendor's newer model
options.C: A model's verdict on one case says little about other cases
options.D: Its design document would be stronger evidence than a test

questions.key_concept: A model's verdicts are learned, not programmed, so one test case cannot stand for other inputs; test AI controls on varied samples.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the planned test would and would not show.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing one transaction suits a programmed control, which applies the same fixed logic to every input. A language model's verdicts are learned, so pinning the version keeps the screen stable but does not make one result predict others; an order naming the chemical another way may pass. The auditor needs a varied sample of orders with known answers. Proof that the screen ran through the year shows operation, not correct judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because automated controls must operate through the period. But tested change controls over the pinned version support that, and running through the year says nothing about judging orders correctly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because newer models can perform better. But pinning a version under tested change controls is sound practice; a newer model would need its own testing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because design shows intent. But a document cannot show how the screen behaves, and testing is stronger evidence of operation than inspection.

tips: Eliminate: B treats pinning a version under tested change controls as a flaw, and D prefers a design document to testing, which is weaker evidence.
Final two: C beats A because change controls support the screen running through the year; only a varied sample shows whether a model's learned verdicts are right.
Exam cue: The test-of-one approach fits programmed controls. Test an AI control on a varied sample with known answers.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.1 Testing AI Controls and Human Oversight (test operation with records; one walkthrough suits programmed logic, but a model's learned verdicts need a varied sample). Round 1 completeness fix: re-angled from hidden instructions in a supplier's upload, which repeated aaia_d2_083's key and runner-up (and aaia_d2_016's threat), to the test-of-one approach for automated controls applied to a model-based screen. Nearest items: aaia_d2_122 (one-language jailbreak tests; test-of-one appears only as a distractor), aaia_d3_028 (reworded bypasses of an output filter) and aaia_d2_159 (repeat runs against more questions); here the runner-up is population coverage, which only the learned-verdict fact defeats. Round 2 fix: option A moved from per-order coverage to operation through the year, so it no longer reads like the key's point about other orders; the tested change controls in the stem answer it. Round 3 fix: the key's 'order' echo of the stem changed to 'case', and option B's explanation and tip 1 now say the change controls were tested, not the version, as the stem gives. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Design of a drift control
questions.question: A Norwegian ferry operator's drift control alerts when its passenger-demand model's weekly forecast error, scored against tickets sold, passes a fixed limit; most summer sailings sell out. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The fixed limit may raise too many alerts in busy weeks
options.B: It measures forecast error rather than shifts in input data
options.C: Weekly checks may not catch a sudden drop in time
options.D: Travelers turned away by full ships never count as error

questions.key_concept: Error scored against capped outcomes, such as sales on full sailings, can hide how far demand outran a forecast.
questions.pre_read: Test each option against what the control is meant to catch.
questions.correct_explanation: On a sold-out sailing, sales stop at capacity, so the figure the forecast is scored against is capped. When demand outruns both the forecast and capacity, measured error understates the miss, so on the busiest sailings, where under-forecasting matters most, drift can grow without an alert. Watching input data could warn earlier, but scoring forecast error is sound design; its flaw is that the outcome scored is capped.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because noisy alerts are a cost. But the risk here is missing a decline on full sailings, not raising too many alerts.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because input drift can warn early. But scoring forecast error is sound design; the problem is that capped sales understate it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because faster checks catch problems sooner. But checks at any frequency scored against capped sales would understate the same misses.

tips: Eliminate: C changes how often the check runs, not what it scores against, and A worries about too many alerts when the risk is too few.
Final two: D beats B because scoring error is right; scoring it against sales capped at capacity hides how far demand outran the forecast.
Exam cue: Ask whether the outcome a model is scored on can show its misses. Capped outcomes hide them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 4.3 (Performance improvements or declines identified and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B.1 Testing AI Controls and Human Oversight (test a drift control's design against what it must catch; error scored against capped outcomes understates misses). Round 1 fix: re-angled from a moving baseline (a frame already used in aaia_d2_156 and aaia_d1_148) to outcomes capped at capacity. Round 2 fix: key reworded so it no longer carries the only reason clause or restates the stem. Round 3 fix: C reworded as a hedged negative so the key is not the only negated option; key_concept now states the capped-outcome condition exactly.
